subject: [framework] Validate SIWE fields in Ethereum DAA (#20589)
body:
construct_message builds the SIWE/EIP-191 preimage by raw byte
concatenation, placing the transaction digest between the unvalidated
scheme and issued_at fields. Both accept newlines and the literal
"Nonce: " / "Issued At: " delimiters, so the field boundary can be
shifted until two distinct transaction digests produce a byte-identical
signed message. One secp256k1 signature then authenticates multiple
distinct transactions, breaking the one-signature-one-transaction
binding the Nonce field is supposed to provide.

Validate scheme, issued_at, domain and ethereum_address at the
deserialization boundary so the encoding is injective again. The
constructed message is unchanged for conforming input, so wallets and
the SDK are unaffected. Also reject MessageV1 explicitly: it has been
unable to authenticate since the scheme field was introduced.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>
rationale: The change adds strict validation of SIWE fields and rejects MessageV1, fixing a flaw where unvalidated scheme/issued_at/domain allowed newline injection and delimiter shifting, enabling a single secp256k1 signature to authenticate multiple distinct transactions (signature replay). This is a security bug with potential fund loss, thus a critical security fix.

subject: [prover] Make Boogie name rendering injective (#20610)
body:
Boogie names were built by joining their parts with a bare `_`, a character a
Move identifier may contain, so distinct Move entities could render to one
name: `0x42::a::b_c` and `0x42::a_b::c` both became `$42_a_b_c`. The emission
loops deduplicated on that rendered name, so the second entity was dropped in
silence and the surviving declaration served both -- one function's body
discharged the other's obligation, and two resource types shared one `$Memory`.
A true postcondition became unprovable and a false one was proved.

- Address, module, entity, variant, spec fun and spec var names now join with
  `.`, which a Move identifier cannot contain. The ~362 names hardcoded in the
  Boogie prelude templates and in Rust are renamed to match.
- The four emission dedups are keyed on the entity (`EmittedEntities`), not the
  rendered name, so a non-injective rendering can no longer delete an
  obligation; a surviving collision is reported once through `GlobalEnv::error`.
  Keys are normalized so function types differing only in abilities -- one
  Boogie entity -- are not reported.
- `boogie_field_sel` joined field and variant with `_`, so field `a` of variant
  `B_C`, field `a_B` of variant `C`, and a ghost field `a_B_C` all rendered
  `$a_B_C`; same-typed fields merged silently. Now joined with `.`.
- The variant `$Update` name was `_<type>_<field>`, and rendered function types
  contain `_`; it is now `_<field>.<type>`, field first because a field name
  contains no `.` while a rendered type does.
- `fun_type` rendered `$fun_<params>_<results>`, so `|u64,u8|u8` and
  `|u64|(u8,u8)` collided; the arities are now part of the name, and
  `translate_fun_type` gained the entity-keyed dedup it lacked.
- Two parsers of generated names are updated: the global-memory name
  extraction in `boogie_wrapper` (which panicked on dotted names, now a tested
  `global_memory_struct_name`) and `humanize_legacy_definition_qid`.

Scope: the joins above are now recoverable. The element join inside
`boogie_inst_suffix` and the tuple suffix is still `_`; a fusion there needs
two same-arity element lists whose concatenations agree, which is not
constructible with current element suffixes.

This makes unconditional the `$Global` resource-type guarantee of the parent
change, which held only while resource types rendered to distinct names.

Regression tests, each failing without its fix: boogie_name_injectivity,
boogie_name_injectivity_structs, boogie_name_injectivity_variants,
boogie_field_sel_injectivity, boogie_variant_update_injectivity,
fun_type_arity_injectivity; plus unit tests of `EmittedEntities::insert`,
which fail if it reverts to name-keyed dedup.

Tested: move-prover testsuite 397 passed, 0 failed; boogie-backend lib tests
46 passed; all four aptos-framework prover suites pass with 0 prover errors;
clippy under the xclippy flag set and nightly fmt are clean.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The change makes Boogie name rendering injective, fixing collisions that previously caused distinct Move entities to be merged and obligations to be silently dropped, leading to false postconditions being proved. This bug could let insecure contracts pass verification, a security-relevant defect.

subject: [mono-move] Crypto algebra natives (#20530)
body:
Port all 23 `0x1::crypto_algebra::*_internal` natives, so Move code over
BLS12-381 and BN254 loads on MonoMove.

The bar is behavioural parity with the legacy VM, down to whether an
abort carries a message: the differential harness renders `code N (msg)`
against `code N`, so a spurious message is observable. Two ordering
subtleties matter. `multi_scalar_mul` and `multi_pairing` match their
type arguments before checking vector lengths, so an unsupported group
with mismatched lengths is "not implemented" rather than a size
mismatch. `order` aborts without a message on an unknown marker, since
legacy's feature-flag check rejects it before reaching the messaged arm.

Natives dispatch polymorphically and resolve their marker structs from
the interned type, which allocates nothing. The empty-type-argument
guard is load-bearing: legacy matches a canonical type string, so it
resolves an instantiated `Fr<u8>` to nothing, and MonoMove must too.

`AlgebraStore` follows `RistrettoPointStore`. One index space holds
every element type, because `upcast` and `downcast` hand back the
caller's handle. Each entry carries the running byte total, which keeps
a checkpoint a single watermark and the 1 MB limit exact.

The four arkworks natives legacy runs under `with_native_rayon` carry a
`TODO(correctness)`: MonoMove cannot depend on `aptos-native-interface`
yet. That is liveness under Block-STM, not correctness, so it does not
affect parity.

Four differential test files cover both curves, all 18 serialization
formats, and the abort paths. The 24 framework unit tests that reported
`Unsupported` now pass.

subject: [verification] Verify Move sources and the standard library with Leaner (#20621)
body:
* [verification] Verify Move sources with Leaner

Leaner verification grows from single fixtures to Move and Rust sources,
Move packages, the Move standard library, and intrinsic maps, and runs from
the Move CLI.

**Source verification**

- `leaner-move verify` and `leaner-rust verify` render sources as
  LeanerLang, verify every specified function, and report messages at the
  original positions, followed by the wall time per phase:
  ```
  $ leaner-move verify sources/proofs.move
  leaner-move: 0.84s load, 0.16s frontend, ..., 0.17s verification, total 1.37s
  $ leaner-move verify my_pkg --filter vector --heartbeats 400
  $ leaner-rust verify bounds.rs      # specifications in bounds.spec.lean
  ```
- From the Move CLI, logging build, export, and verifier times:
  `move prove --lean --package-dir my_pkg`.
- A function the automatic verification leaves open is proved in a proof
  file beside its source; the failure message names the file, and
  `verify f by skip` shows the obligations left:
  ```move
  spec square_of_sum { pragma verify = manual; ... }   // proofs.move
  ```
  ```lean
  verify square_of_sum by                               -- proofs.proof.lean
    case leaf_1 => ...
  ```
- `pragma heartbeats = N` (function or module) and `--heartbeats` set the
  budget; `pragma verify = manual` requires a proof. The Move Prover
  ignores `heartbeats` and reads `verify = manual` as true.

**Modules**

- Validated namespaces are relocatable (R1) and linked without
  re-validation (R2); verification inlines across modules.

**Move Prover semantics**

- Callees are inlined unless native, opaque, or on a cycle, with one fixed
  point per cycle; `[abstract]`/`[concrete]` views; native models; range
  and vector quantifiers; spec `let`; address aliases; `pragma bv` leaves
  decided by `bv_decide`.

**Intrinsic maps**

- The Prover's map roles are read over a map model proved in Lean (sorted
  entries for ordered maps, insertion order for SimpleMap), with
  `cmp::compare` as the structural order; ordered_map verifies with its
  iterator tests. The closer adds the facts an SMT solver's map axioms
  would give at the positions a leaf reads.

**Standard library**

- option, vector, fixed_point32, error, bit_vector, and the bit flags of
  features verify; the verify suite records the rest.

**Closer**

- Quantified leaves decided at an instance, range invariants extended by
  one step, bounds asserted once, saturation to a fixed point.

**Performance**

- ordered_map 300 s → 82 s: generic frame certificates shared by type
  identity (`frameInstantiation_congr`), lifetime kinds read through an
  index, and variant splits renormalizing only what they change.
- Normalize only what a step creates, rewrite the denotation by its
  equations, index arenas for the kernel-checked certificates, precompute
  interface spelling, traverse shared terms once.
- Lean CI: `lowerExpr` split into functions (its C compile 264 s → 23 s);
  the e2e check suite runs beside source verification.
- `designs/perf-notes.md` records measurements, rejected experiments, the
  plan to prove the preparation certificates once, and the tools:
  ```
  set_option leaner.stageLog "/tmp/m.stage"            -- stage times per target
  $ scripts/isolate-target.py m.lean ordered_map f -o f.lean
  $ scripts/exp-error-delta.sh                         # error deltas after UB=1
  ```

**Compiler and docs**

- Leaner modules compile to Move bytecode through an LIR-to-XIR backend.
- README.md documents the verify commands, flags, pragmas, and proof files.
- `designs/roadmap.md` is the single status document with the test ledger;
  executed designs move to `designs/historical/`.

- `pragma intrinsic` disables verification only where the Move Prover's

  aggregator, aggregator_v2), or an opaque function. Elsewhere the body is

- The XIR backend passes a struct's or function's source attributes, such
  as `module_lock` and `persistent`, to compiler-v2; modifiers XIR carries

- The axiom audit re-evaluates a `bv_decide` certificate natively instead
  of accepting any axiom with its name and shape (fixture

- The verifiers print their wall time per phase on stderr, so the
  `prove --lean` baselines keep only the verifier's messages; the Move CLI

A LeanerLang module lowered against another module's interface could call

resolveLocalRef now applies Move's rule to a call into another Move module:
public from anywhere, friend from a module the callee's module names a
friend, package from a module at its address (Move compiles package

declaration, so it could call a private function of another module. Typed
calls are now reserved for namespaces the unit does not hold.

The exporter recorded a function constructing a closure as skipped, but the
encoder discarded every skip whose reason named the function, so the function
vanished and source verification succeeded without it. The exporter now
leaves out only inline functions, which compiler-v2 expands at their call
sites; the encoder keeps every skip, and source verification reports each as
an error.

XIR lowered a match by taking its last arm unconditionally, assuming
validation proved coverage, which it does not. A match missing a variant now
fails to lower, as Move rejects it.

subject: [prover] compare insertion-ordered intrinsic maps by position (#20666)
body:
* [prover] compare insertion-ordered intrinsic maps by position

* [prover] regression test for insertion-ordered map equality

Pins the behaviour the previous commit introduced, on a self-contained
intrinsic map bound through the insertion-ordered role pair rather than
through `simple_map`, so the test exercises the mechanism and not one
library's use of it.

Four cases, and the baseline records the split between them:

- two maps holding the same entries inserted in opposite orders are not
  equal -- the defect, which verified before the fix;
- a map equals itself, so the position conjunct has not made equality
  unusable;
- the rank/key_at facts still hold, since the conjunct does not disturb
  the order-agnostic part of the enumeration;
- `ensures false` fails, so suppressing the ascending-under-`cmp` axiom
  has not left the state inconsistent. A false axiom here would make
  callers vacuous rather than fail, so this one is load-bearing.

Verified to be a real detector rather than a decoration: with the role
pair swapped to the key-ordered `map_spec_key_at` / `map_spec_rank`, the
equality case verifies again and the defect reproduces.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [prover] do not assume removal shifts ranks in an insertion-ordered map

The removal-shift axiom says a surviving key's rank drops by one exactly
when it sat above the removed key. That is order-preserving removal, and
it is not what an insertion-ordered map has to do: `simple_map::remove`
calls `swap_remove`, moving the last entry into the vacated position, so
surviving ranks do not shift at all.

Binding the insertion enumeration therefore emitted an axiom that
contradicts the implementation. No exploit was found -- two probes, one
over `spec_insertion_key_at` and one over `spec_insertion_rank`, both
failed to derive a runtime-false order fact from it -- but a trusted
axiom that disagrees with the code it models is a latent hazard in a
position where the failure mode is vacuous proofs rather than visible
errors, and the equality conjunct added by the previous commit does
reference the enumeration, so removal paths are reachable in principle.

So the axiom is now emitted for key-ordered maps only. Suppressing it
cannot introduce unsoundness, it can only cost provability: a rank after
a removal becomes unconstrained, which makes dependent facts unprovable
rather than wrong. Nothing currently depends on one -- aptos-stdlib
still proves 421 of 421, including pool_u64 and its removal paths, and
the regression fixture still matches its baseline.

Corrects the previous commit message and the PR description, both of
which claimed every rank shift axiom was order-agnostic. That holds for
the insertion shift, which is vacuous when new keys append, and for
value-write rank preservation, which reorders nothing. It does not hold
for removal, which this commit stops assuming.

Reported by cursor[bot] on the pull request.

subject: [verification] Leaner: higher-order functions, state labels, static memory, invariants (#20681)
body:
* [verification] Leaner: higher-order functions, state labels, static memory, invariants

Extends the Leaner verifier (`third_party/move/lean`) toward the Move
Prover's test suite, which now runs under Leaner with
`MVP_TEST_FEATURE=lean` (`.lean_exp` baselines; the open problems are
registered in `designs/prover-test-problems.md`).

- Higher-order functions: a rule for invoking a function value the proof
  does not see, read through the behavioral predicates (`ensures_of`,
  `aborts_of`, `result_of`); function values named in specifications;
  frames of function-valued parameters (`modifies_of`); termination as an
  assumption where `result_of` is read; spec-less lambdas read by their
  bodies.
- Function values as typed carriers (design: `higher-order-functions.md`,
  "Closures in memory"): a function type's values are the closures whose
  target has its signature at their frame, typed in native types. Compiled
  code, memory, and executables are indexed by their unit; a closure of a
  generic target is typed at a frame coherent with its runtime type
  instantiation; generic public theorems hold at every coherent
  instantiation. Native types read as semantic types (`TypesAgree`,
  decided per unit); nominal types record their type arguments, so phantom
  parameters keep types apart. Function values are typed by their
  carriers, so contracts no longer assume their typing, and memory with
  function-typed fields is typed.
- State labels (design: `state-labels.md`, S1–S3b): labels of Move
  specifications (`..S |~ …`, `exists S in *`) round-trip through the
  exchange, LIR, and LeanerLang; quantified labels are memory binders in
  contracts, with copies of `&mut` parameters per label; the closer
  witnesses them from the program points of the body (`ProgramPoint`
  hypotheses) and from the bounds a clause states. Specification types
  see through references.
- Static global memory: one typed memory per resource type, read at
  induced frames by callers.
- Invariants: data invariants of stored resources and where mutations end,
  module invariants of every module of the unit by memory reach, in-body
  assertions as cuts with state anchors, in-body assumptions as theorem
  hypotheses.
- Specifications: lemmas and proof blocks, mutually recursive spec
  functions, typed aggregate values, tuples, vectors and slices, bitwise
  operations, division facts where a leaf reads them, hashes, signers,
  spec functions over `&mut` parameters and generic storage reads, variant
  field selections that name their variants.
- Patterns: matches and refutable patterns with Move's mismatch aborts,
  patterns through references.
- Soundness and borrowing: lexical scoping of Move locals (same-name locals
  were merged), units the borrow analysis rejects are refused, loans end
  where their holder is overwritten.
- Exchange and tooling: intrinsic vector functions as LIR operations,
  module axioms exported, `move prove --lean` tests in the CLI, the
  verification benchmark's problems and report page. XIR version 8 adds
  function types and the closure operations; the XIR type checker types
  them, and a function's used and called sets both come from its
  translated code.

- `leaner-ir`, `leaner-move`, `leaner-rust`, and `leaner-e2e-tests` suites,
  with new Check fixtures per feature (e.g. `Closures/Carriers`,
  `Closures/Frames`, `Closures/GenericHofs`, `Storage/GenericSpecReads`)
  and the verification-cost gate (`DenotePerformance`).
- Move Prover tests under `MVP_TEST_FEATURE=lean`: 112 of 414 verify.
- Verification benchmark (`scripts/leaner-bench.py`): 24 of 32 problems
  verify; the two higher-order paper examples are in the set before they
  verify. `designs/handoff.md` records where to resume.

- `leaner-ir/LeanerIR/Proofs/Denote/Types.lean`: native types, carriers,
  closure admission, frames.
- `leaner-ir/LeanerIR/Proofs/GlobalTyping.lean` and `ClosureTyping.lean`:
  native and semantic readings, memory typing, carrier typing.
- `leaner-ir/LeanerIR/Proofs/Denote/Close.lean`: the closer, including the
  unseen-invocation rule and transports between frames.
- `leaner-ir/LeanerLang/Contract.lean` and `Verify.lean`: generated
  contracts and theorems.

subject: [trading-native][vm] Wire native-position writes through VMChangeSet + finalize (#20570)
body:
VM-side plumbing that carries native-position writes from the
session extension into the transaction output, plus the match arms
that downstream consumers need for the `StateKeyInner::TradingNative`
(Position) variant.

aptos-vm-types:
- `VMChangeSet.position_write_set`: a dedicated bucket for Position
  writes that never enters the flat WriteSet value bucket.
  `set_position_bucket` validates every key is a TradingNative
  Position key. Squash is last-wins per key; creation+deletion
  pairs are not collapsed because the position store is an
  idempotent key/value map. Unit tests cover the validation and
  the last-wins squash.
- `VMOutput` materialization drains the bucket into the WriteSet's
  `native_positions` sibling bucket (as `NativePositionOp`); the storage
  commit applier consumes it via `WriteSet::native_position_iter`. The
  write set is upgraded with `into_v1()` when the bucket is non-empty:
  `freeze()` yields V0, whose extension bucket is `#[serde(skip)]`, so
  without the upgrade the positions would be dropped at every
  serialization boundary (write-set replay, output sync, remote
  execution). Position writes are also counted in `materialized_size`,
  so the per-block output size limit accounts for them.

aptos-vm:
- Session finalize (`respawned_session`/`finish`) drains the
  `NativePositionContext` extension via `into_change_maps()`,
  converts it with `build_position_writeset` (NativePosition
  payload -> `WriteOp::legacy_creation`; `None` ->
  `legacy_deletion`), and routes it through `set_position_bucket`.
- The session builder installs the `NativePositionContext` extension,
  as does the Move unit-test extension hook. (Move-side reads of native
  state are not part of this change.)
- `try_combine_into_storage_change_set` returns a code invariant error
  if the position bucket is non-empty rather than dropping it; the
  bucket is drained by `VMOutput` via `take_position_write_set` before
  combining, so the non-`VMOutput` callers (e2e `FakeExecutor`,
  vm-genesis, release-builder simulate) can no longer silently lose
  position writes.
- `ChangeSetInterface::num_position_write_ops` plus a

subject: [mono-move] Create the sender's account lazily, from Move
body:
A first transaction from an address holding no Account resource creates
the account before the payload runs, as AptosVM does. Unlike AptosVM,
the creation is Move code: a new metered half of the prologue,
transaction_validation::versioned_metered_prologue, runs after the
prologue has validated the transaction and before the payload, charged
against the gas budget. Its effects sit before the payload's checkpoint,
so a rolled-back payload keeps them; AptosVM reaches the same effects by
re-creating the account in a separate abort-hook session. A failure
there discards the transaction, again as AptosVM does.

The executor thus makes no account-specific Move call: new pre-payload
state setup is a new MeteredPrologueArgs variant and a framework change,
not executor logic. What remains in Rust is the budget check that the
gas can pay for the account's storage slot, which needs the storage
pricing Move cannot read, and the unmetered existence read that triggers
it.

Alternative to #20566, which creates the account from Rust.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit moves lazy account creation from Rust to Move and adds a gas budget check for the storage slot, fixing a prior situation where account creation could occur without proper metering, which could be exploited for free storage and DoS. This change corrects the behavior and addresses a security issue related to uncontrolled resource consumption.

subject: [framework] large_packages: position-keyed chunks
body:
Each staged chunk is now kept in its own storage slot, keyed by its
position: part 0 is the package metadata and part i + 1 is module i.
Staging a chunk no longer reads back and rewrites the module it
extends, or other modules sharing its SmartTable bucket, and the
StagingArea resource stays small instead of holding the metadata.

- New stage_chunks* entry functions take each chunk's position, so
  chunks can be staged in any order. Staging a chunk again is a no-op,
  a different chunk at a taken position aborts with ECHUNK_CONFLICT,
  and the final call takes the number of chunks in each part and
  aborts with EMISSING_CHUNK or EUNEXPECTED_CHUNKS.
- The stage_code_chunk* functions are kept for existing clients and
  append to the same storage.
- cleanup_staging_area does nothing when nothing is staged.
- The CLI reads the module at the target address and uses
  stage_chunks* when it has them, else stage_code_chunk* (mainnet's
  deployment and networks created before this change).
  clear-staging-area no longer submits a transaction when nothing is
  staged.
- Measured against the previous module in a local simulation, staging
  and publishing a 786 KB package takes 26% less execution and IO gas
  (36% less IO).
- Regenerate head.mrb.
rationale: The commit changes large package staging to use position-keyed storage slots, fixing a crash/DoS caused by resource bloat and unintended rewrites. This addresses an availability issue, qualifying as a security fix.

subject: [cli] Resume incomplete chunked publishes
body:
When a chunked publish stopped partway (a failed or interrupted
transaction), the next run cleared the staged chunks and staged them
all again. With a large_packages module that stages chunks by position
(stage_chunks), the CLI now reads what the sender has staged and only
submits the chunks that are missing.

- A staged chunk is reused only if it is byte-for-byte identical to
  the chunk of this package at the same position, since skipping a
  stale chunk would publish an old version of the package. If any
  staged chunk differs or has no counterpart, or the resource is not
  laid out like a StagingArea, it is cleared as before.
- Works for publish, upgrade-object-package and upgrade-object. A
  publish to a new object is not resumed: the object address depends
  on the number of transactions, so a rerun builds different chunks.
- The in-order stage_code_chunk functions (mainnet's deployment) are
  unchanged: they cannot tell what is staged, so stale data is cleared.
- chunked_publish: PositionalChunks (chunks sorted by position, the
  chunks still missing, the chunk key layout shared with the module)
  and a builder that stages any subset of a package's chunks.
- Tests: builder unit tests, and mock-chain tests for resuming after
  some chunks, with only the publishing transaction left, and for
  clearing chunks of another package, chunks the package does not
  have, and an empty StagingArea.
rationale: The commit changes the chunked publish resume logic to correctly reuse only identical staged chunks, fixing a bug where previously all chunks were cleared and re‑staged. The change does not address a security vulnerability; it merely restores correct behavior and improves efficiency.

subject: [framework] Model the transaction counter as strictly increasing in specs
body:
`monotonically_increasing_counter` packs timestamp, transaction index,
session counter and local counter, most significant first, so each value it
returns exceeds every earlier one. Its spec said nothing about the value,
so a caller could not show that a value it draws differs from one it
stored earlier, e.g. that a fresh priority index cannot collide with an
existing key.

A spec global `spec_counter_last` records the last value returned; each
call returns a value above it and updates it. The increase is stated only
below `MAX_U128`; an unguarded form is inconsistent, since nothing exceeds
the top of the range.

Like the existing `aborts_if [abstract] false`, these are trusted facts
about a native. Verify and the consistency check pass on
`transaction_context` and on the callers in `aptos-trading` and
`aptos-experimental` that have verification roots.
rationale: The change only updates a specification file to model the transaction counter as strictly increasing; it does not modify runtime code or fix a security-relevant defect.

  the only dead code in the module.
- Docs: the module documentation now describes parts, chunks and

  cleaning up, the legacy functions, and the abort codes. Every item

subject: [prover] Verex: Prover parity, authored proofs; rename Leaner to Verex (#20710)
body:
* [prover] Leaner: Prover parity, invariants, authored proofs

Closes many of the gaps the Move Prover's unit tests show under the Leaner
verifier (`MVP_TEST_FEATURE=lean`); remaining gaps are recorded in
designs/prover-test-problems.md and designs/handoff.md.

Specification semantics
- The Prover's bit-vector representation is treated as a backend
  encoding: specification arithmetic stays mathematical, int2bv/bv2int
  are exact.
- A specification function is defined where its parameters fit their
  declared fixed-width types and unspecified elsewhere.
- Module axioms are assumed globally; generic axioms and generic module
  invariants are monomorphized as the Prover does, with ghost type
  parameters for written memory a function does not fix.
- bcs::serialize facts of the Prover's prelude (injective, nonempty,
  constant address length) hold of serialized parameters.

Calls and preconditions
- Callers owe a callee's preconditions also where its body is inlined;
  a function without a specification is verified when it calls one with
  a precondition.
- Inline functions with a specification of their own are verified.
- Callers of a callee whose verification failed or did not run assume its
  contract, as in the Prover; the callee's failure stays reported, and a
  callee still in progress is refused as circular.

Function values
- aborts_of, ensures_of and result_of over functions with &mut
  parameters, in the Prover's argument layout; behaviors of capturing
  closures read through their target.
- Behavioral predicates of targets returning &mut read the result as a
  value at return; result_of of a lent invocation is unique.
- Behavioral predicates are witnessed under state labels; closure runs
  are read once per conjunction and at struct and enum arguments.

Mutable references
- A &mut a call returns that no local holds is bound to a local of its
  own, so its current value settles into the lender.
- A mutable place borrow that dies where it is used (dereferenced, read
  through, compared, discarded) is read as a shared borrow of its place
  once the borrow analysis has checked it, keeping its conflicts.
- Comparisons read references as their referents; loan independence
  covers injective renamings of loans and starts that lend references.
- A reference type's instantiation fingerprint distinguishes its kind and
  profile.

Frontend and driver
- `--verify-only` / `--only` select targets; scripts and quoted module
  names are verified; misplaced loop invariants are rejected and a loop's
  specification blocks are joined.
- Sound loop unrolling reports an exhausted bound.
- Table values, caller-side state labels, field updates through
  references, and nested invocation results.

Solver
- Cheaper witness search, bitwise identities, timed pipeline stages.
- A loop invariant is normalized once as a predicate; the loop step
  normalizes its instances only around their clauses.
- A range invariant extended by an iteration is decided at the new
  element through the context's position invariants.
- A split attempt normalizes the context only where the normalized goal
  has something to split, by the stage normalization.
- A hypothesis's normal form and its rewrite rules are reused across the
  leaves of a target.

Benchmark: suite totals include rejected work, labels in Pacific time.

Authored proofs
- An authored proof receives the function's whole goal; `leaner_obligations`
  splits it into one goal per clause (a conjunction over the paths that owe
  it), `leaner_paths` into path goals, and `leaner_on` dispatches by
  clause. Hand-over leaves keep their own conditionals, which removes the
  per-path re-proof of each clause (benchmark -3.8%).
- Every Leaner tactic acts on the main goal (`focusGoal`), fixing a dropped
  goal that Lean reported as an unsynthesized `post` placeholder. The
  solver is renamed from "closer".
- In the editor, `verify` items are skipped unless marked `verify!` (code
  action "Verify `f` here"); `leaner.skip_verify` detects the language
  server since Lake does not pass `moreServerOptions` to library modules
  (leanprover/lean4#15626).

Frames
- A function with a body that declares no contract and plays no map or
  table role claims no frame: it is verified for the invariants it writes,
  and its callers inline it. Writers of resources with stored closures
  verify (compiler-v2 `leaner/closures`), and so does
  `lambda_captured_fun_loop::wrap2`.

CI runs the Rust exporter's own tests.

subject: [prover] Verex: proof files with a working InfoView; Table owners as owned values (#20746)
body:
* [prover] Verex: proof files as Lean files with a working InfoView

A Move proof file (`foo.proof.lean`) is now a Lean file whose header
loads its module's context, so it opens in the editor with goals:

    import VerexMove.Proofs
    verex proofs for "foo.move"
    verex proofs where

The module command registers; its verification is a separate step the
proof file runs with the file's items (`verex proofs where`), as the
driver does after registering the module with verification deferred.
Each proof file sees only its module and the modules rendered before it.
In the editor the header loads the rendering the last verification wrote
and warns when a source changed since; an edit re-elaborates the items
alone. Messages about the rendering are relocated to the item that
raised them (`verex.relocateMessages`, off in the driver).

verex-move places renderings: `build/verex-verify.lean` of a package,
`build/verex/<path>.lean` of the package around a single file, `.verex/`
beside a file of no package. Lake workspaces at the three trees holding
proof files; e2e `<name>.proof.exp` baselines check the editor path.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [prover] Verex: Table owners as owned values

A table owner's value holds its entries in a hidden last field, so the
denotation reads a table's contents off its value, and every executable and
specification role is available for table layouts. The runtime boundary
erases the field into native storage; tables are to become values in the
runtime semantics as well, which removes that boundary.

Allocation takes a fresh handle recorded in an allocation history that
callers' frames leave open, and specification equality over values holding
tables compares identities. The solver checks the data invariants of values
written to memory as their own clause, canonicalizes carrier spellings,
evaluates ground bitwise literals, folds appends of literal vectors, and
normalizes a cut's hypothesis again after the substitutions that fix its
values.

subject: Fix resource account recreation (#20356)
body:
This fixes the SignerCapability duplication vulnerability where an attacker
could create multiple capabilities for the same resource account by exploiting
the revoke-and-recreate pattern.

Changes:
- Remove the account takeover logic that allowed recreation after revocation
- Add strict check that Account resource must not exist at derived address
- Update doc comments to reflect the security-focused design
- Update test to expect failure when Account already exists (the secure behavior)
- Regenerate cached packages with updated framework code

The previous takeover mechanism was the root cause of CVE findings in
delegation pools and multisig. This fix prevents SignerCapability duplication
by disallowing recreation once an Account resource exists.
rationale: The diff removes the ability to recreate a resource account after revocation, which previously allowed an attacker to duplicate SignerCapability and gain unauthorized access. This corrects a security flaw (access control) and prevents privilege escalation.

subject: [prover] Verex maps and bounded proof automation (#20755)
body:
Keep table storage native at runtime while verifying intrinsic maps through
abstract values. Make automatic proofs cheap and predictable, with direct
authored proofs for obligations that need a mathematical argument.

- Execute native table roles over handle-based storage and carry the locality
  assumptions needed to relate runtime storage to verification values. Every
  executable role has a runtime step, the entry roles (iter_borrow_mut,
  new_with_config, to_ordered_map) included; the roles are named once in
  VerexIR (MapOperation, MapSpecRole) for the runtime, the contracts and the
  Move registry. Abort codes are the VM's: the table natives' legacy
  encoding, and `error::invalid_state(102)` for checked destruction, in the
  Lean runtime and the Boogie prelude alike; `map_destroy_unchecked`
  declares the native that never checks.
- A mutable reference copied by name into a binding or an assignment is
  normalized at validation like a call argument: a move where the copy is
  the local's last executable use, a reborrow otherwise, so no two locals
  hold one loan and a write through the copy reaches the caller. Escaping
  references need established caller provenance.
- Carry ghost fields, specification variables and closure targets through the
  unit model; support abstract map owners, validity slots and literal maps.
  Ghost initializers bind the declaration locals invariants use; a
  fixed-width value may update a mathematical ghost.
- Provide a typed SpecMap model with a separate encoding boundary, selective
  map lifting, source-named hypotheses and laws, and useful proof templates.
- Bound each complete automatic leaf attempt at 20M heartbeats. Authored
  proofs bypass automatic search unless they explicitly request it.
- Share preparation before clause splitting and group compatible contexts.
  Add and simplify map and corpus proofs using direct laws, targeted
  normalization and arithmetic instead of repeated general search.
- Split solveGoals and verifyMember into small step functions to reduce Lean
  code-generation time (downstream rebuild 4m24s to 1m44s at that
  refactor's measurement).
- Add scripts/smoke.sh and its workflow for fast, read-only validation between
  edit batches. Keep the full suites as the checkpoint gate.
- Isolate the Move Prover Lean gate from concurrent builds by snapshotting
  the verifier's executable and imported modules, retried while sources or

subject: [prover] Order facts for key-ordered maps, closure frames through generic callees, and congruence for behavioral predicates (#20740)
body:
Seven prover changes and one framework specification that a downstream
package needs together.

A. Order facts for key-ordered maps read by position. A use of the sorted
   `spec_key_at` with key `K` registers `cmp::compare<K>` (only when the
   custom natives template declares the comparison model). The first and
   last positions bound every contained key, and each insertion template
   names the previous end keys as still contained. Both apply only when
   comparing `K` never walks a vector or an intrinsic map. Also closes a
   false assumption on `main`: `map_keys`/`map_to_vec_pair` assumed
   ascending keys for insertion-ordered maps.

B. Closure frames through generic opaque callees. An opaque callee with a
   function-typed parameter and no `modifies_of`/`reads_of` for it may
   leave that parameter's frame to the call site, but only when its body
   is never proven and its specification names no global memory; a
   forwarded, joined, or loop-built callback still errors. What the
   closure writes is what a call to its target writes as the prover
   encodes it (the declared frame for a native or unverified opaque
   target, the usage summary otherwise); only a closure whose target has
   such known effects, is not the enclosing function, and does not itself
   defer, can be deferred to. Those effects are carried into the usage
   summary of the function making the call and into the havoc of a loop
   containing it. A target that invokes a function value no check bounds
   (anything but its own parameter, declared or of an opaque function)
   has unknown effects, so its closure is rejected on both the deferred
   and the declared-frame path; so is any closure built at the call site
   whose effects are otherwise unknown (a wildcard invoke frame, a target
   that defers its own closure frame, or the enclosing function). A closure
   over an opaque unverified target is charged with what a direct call to
   it havocs: its declared frame plus what its body writes. A closure
   whose target has a function-typed parameter has no known footprint: the
   target bounds invoking that parameter only by the check a direct call
   makes on the argument, and a closure's target gets it unchecked, from
   the captures or from whoever invokes the closure. A closure
   whose target updates a spec variable is not deferred either: a call-site
   havoc never covers a spec variable. Deferral only adds to the call-site havoc:
   every closure built once is still havoced with what its target's summary
   writes, as before, whether or not its effects are known, so a closure the
   frame check does not see (in a dependency) loses nothing. A callee
   defers a parameter's frame only if its body uses the parameter solely by
   invoking it, so the closure runs during the call the havoc covers. Deferral is enabled only for the Boogie
   pipeline; the Lean backend keeps every undeclared closure frame empty.

C. Behavioral predicates give equal answers on equal values. After each
   uninterpreted `aborts_of`/`requires_of` of a function-typed parameter or
   struct field, an axiom says it agrees on `$IsEqual`-equal arguments.
   Withheld when the argument type can carry a ghost field a
   specification may read, since `$IsEqual` ignores ghosts.

D. The transaction counter modelled as an issued sequence
   (framework spec only). A draw count and an uninterpreted, strictly
   increasing `spec_counter_issued(i)`; each call returns the value at the
   current count and advances it.

E. Boogie tuples up to twenty elements, so a callback with more than
   eleven parameters can carry a contract.

F. Value-equality congruence for spec functions spliced from a callee's
   `ensures` into a lambda's derived contract.

G. An opaque call's behavioral aggregates are stated over the memory at
   the call. The `aborts_of`/`ensures_of` assumptions at an opaque call took
   the enclosing function's entry label; they now take a fresh label per
   call, under which the callee's evaluator memory is saved, so a caller's
   `aborts_if aborts_of<callee>(..)` means "the callee, as called, aborts".

Each change has functional tests; see the PR description for the
problem, the change and the negatives per section.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit changes prover handling of closure frames and ordering facts, fixing unsound verification behavior that could allow malicious Move contracts to be incorrectly proven safe. This corrects a bug in the verification tool and mitigates a security risk where attackers could exploit the prior lax checks.

subject: [framework] Loop invariants for BigOrderedMap::for_each_mut (#20814)
body:
The walk's invariant only said the iterator was valid. The map is written
through `&mut` inside the loop, so a caller's proof lost the map's length,
and nothing said the iterator pointed at an entry: the borrow in the loop
body could abort, even over an empty map.

Two invariants, both true because a value write moves no keys: the map's
length does not change, and a non-end iterator points at a key in the map.
A walk over an empty map now provably never runs its closure, and a walk
with a closure that cannot abort is abort-free.

Tests: `test_verify_for_each_mut_empty_symbolic` and
`test_verify_for_each_mut_total_symbolic`; dropping either invariant fails
both. The cached packages are regenerated for the source change.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The change adds loop invariants that guarantee the iterator does not point to an entry when the map is empty, preventing the closure from being called on an empty map (which could abort, e.g., division by zero). This fixes a bug where the map could abort unexpectedly, a denial‑of‑service vector.

subject: [vm] Make runtime type checks O(1) in type size
body:
* [vm] Cache size, depth and abilities on runtime type nodes

Paranoid runtime type checks performed per-instruction work proportional
to the size of a local's runtime type, while gas was only charged for the
concrete value (type size is charged once, at frame creation). A local
holding a single bool can have a 123-node runtime type, so a loop over it
ran ~10-40x slower per gas unit than the same bytecode over a u64. Two
sinks were reported: `create_ref_ty` / `create_vec_ty` rebuilt the whole
inner type on every borrow / VecPack just to recount nodes, and
`Type::abilities` recursively recomputed every type argument's abilities
on every CopyLoc / Pop / Eq / Neq.

Rather than patching those two sinks, make the whole class unwritable:
every compound `Type` node now carries a `TypeInfo` (node count, max
depth, abilities, flags) computed at construction from its children, so
size, depth and ability queries are O(1).

- `TypeInfo` is derived purely from structure and is excluded from
  Eq / Hash / Debug (via `derivative`, like `AbilityInfo`). `Type` stays
  at 56 bytes.
- References switch from `Box<Type>` to `TriompheArc<TypeNode>`, the same
  representation as `Vector`. `TypeNode` derefs to `Type` so existing
  `Vector(elem_ty)` / `Reference(inner_ty)` patterns keep working, and
  cloning any type is an Arc bump.
- Smart constructors (`Type::vector`, `reference`, `mut_reference`,
  `struct_instantiation`, `function`) compute the metadata in O(children)
  and are the only way production code builds compound types.
- Counts are raw structural counts; the gas-version-dependent
  reference-node adjustments stay in `TypeBuilder`, so the same type
  built under two configs has identical metadata.
- `create_ref_ty` / `create_vec_ty` check limits in O(1) from the cached
  counts and fall back to an exact replica of the old node-by-node walk
  only when a limit may be exceeded, so error codes and size-vs-depth
  precedence are unchanged.
- `Type::abilities` reads the cached byte; the recursive computation
  remains as the fallback for templates containing type parameters.
- `num_nodes` / `num_nodes_with_max_depth` become O(1) (frame-creation
  gas, signature-index cache, constants) with a traversal fallback on
  u16 saturation so gas stays exact; the thread-local memo in
  `num_nodes_in_subst` is removed.

No gas or feature-version gating is needed: metadata is unobservable
from Move, produced types are structurally identical, and every limit
decision and error code is unchanged in all configurations.

Adds unit tests validating cached metadata against traversal, Arc
sharing, exhaustive equivalence of the new limit checks against the old
rebuild across counting modes and limits, cached vs. recursive
abilities, and u16 saturation; plus an e2e regression test comparing the
123-node local against a u64 control for both reported sinks
(7.4x -> 1.09x and 1.04x before/after).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [vm] Add e2e probe quantifying remaining O(type size) per-instruction costs

Six families, each a deep-type variant vs a u64 (or shallow-struct)
control at the same bytecode shape, 300 iterations, best of 3, release
build, production gas schedule. Ratio with paranoid type checks on
(default, as on mainnet) and off:

  family                          on     off    class
  function type clone            1.91x  1.04x  paranoid-check gap: Type::clone
                                       deep-copies Vec args/results
  return handoff compare        3.50x  1.03x  paranoid-check gap: per-call
                                       substitute + structural compare
  generic native arg check      3.04x  0.99x  paranoid-check gap: same,
                                       at the native boundary
  bcs layout-cache key re-intern 1.26x  1.26x  cache path, checker-independent
  type_of tag render             5.75x  5.63x  reflection path, checker-independent
  object_exists resource key    1.14x  1.13x  cache path, checker-independent
                                       (39-node resource: struct-tag
                                       conversion caps resource types)

The paranoid-off control separates the classes: the first three vanish
without the checker (gaps in the checker relative to the cached size/
depth/abilities metadata); the last three persist, since they hash,
intern, or render the runtime type on cache and reflection paths that
run regardless of the checker.

The test prints the ratios; it is a probe, not a regression gate yet.
Deep types enter through generic substitution so signatures stay small
(verifier weights); tag-capped families use 39-node types where the
type-tag pseudo-gas limit (~49 nodes) applies.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [vm] Close remaining O(type size) paranoid-check and cache paths

After the previous change caches size/depth/abilities on every runtime type node,
several per-instruction paths still did work proportional to runtime
type size while gas stayed flat; this makes each of them O(1). Measured
by the paranoid_type_check_gaps probe (deep type vs shallow control,
same bytecode, 300 iterations, best of 3, prod gas schedule), ratios on
Before -> with this change:

  family                          481   now
  function type clone             1.9x  1.1x
  return handoff compare         3.5x  1.1x
  generic native arg check       3.0x  1.1x
  bcs layout-cache key re-intern  1.3x  1.0x
  type_of reflection             5.7x  1.0x
  type_name reflection           3.2x  1.0x
  object_exists resource key     1.1x  1.0x

One mechanism per family:

- Compound type nodes carry a lazily-interned id cell, filled by
  InternedTypePool::instantiate_and_intern only for fully-instantiated
  types. Eq on node payloads short-circuits on id equality (falling
  back to the structural comparison otherwise); Hash stays structural.
  Function nodes share their signature payload behind an Arc (abilities
  stay on the Type::Function variant: they depend on captured values,
  not the signature), so cloning a function type is an Arc bump.
  Reference variants bypass the node cell: their payload Arc is the
  same type Vector uses and is reused across the mutable/immutable
  boundary by paranoid_freeze_ref_ty.
- LoadedFunction memoizes its expected param/return types (definition
  signature, or the instantiation with the fixed type args for generic
  functions, on thread-safe cells shared across Block-STM workers);
  the return handoff, the native-call boundary and the make_call_frame
  parameter check read them instead of re-running create_ty_with_subst
  per call, and check_return_tys interns both compared types.
- The type loader memoizes conversion within one signature-table
  entry, so structurally identical tokens share Arc-backed types.
- TypeTagCache keys on TypeVecId and the transaction data cache on
  TypeId (interned once per load) instead of hashing full types.
- type_of/type_name use a memoized canonical rendering
  (RuntimeEnvironment::ty_to_canonical_string); type_of takes address
  and module name from the interned struct name index. One render on
  first use; the per-byte charge covers exactly that pass.

flush_all_caches documents its precondition instead of enforcing it in
the type layer: flushes happen only between executions (all callers
hold the module cache manager) - the same lifetime discipline
StructNameIndex has always had.

No gas or feature-version gating: every produced type is structurally
identical to what the old paths produced and every cache key is
internal. Regression tests pin the cell invariants (asymmetric
interning keeps Eq/Hash consistent, generic nodes never filled, same
signature with different abilities shares payload but interns
differently, FreezeRef result equals a fresh immutable reference); the
move-vm transactional tests pass with zero .exp changes across
baseline/paranoid/async-paranoid modes, and the block executor suite
passes with the memoized cells sha
rationale: The commit fixes a performance bug where runtime type checks were O(N) in type size, allowing an attacker to craft large types that consume disproportionate CPU for little gas, leading to a potential denial‑of‑service. Caching type metadata makes the checks O(1), mitigating the resource‑consumption issue.

subject: [trading-native][move] Add native_order_book module and order natives (#20821)
body:
Orders need a Move write API into native order storage, as positions
have native_position.

Move: native_order_types declares NativeSingleOrder<M> and
NativeBulkOrder<M> (metadata M last) with constructors, and
native_order_book has set/delete for single and bulk orders, each gated
by TradingNativeCapability::assert_valid.

Rust: a new aptos-order-natives crate with NativeOrderContext, which
stages per-transaction order writes, and the four natives, gated by
NATIVE_ORDERBOOK. An order value is unpacked field by field into the
aptos-types order type, whose writer produces the BCS of the Move
value; only the metadata M is serialized through its runtime layout,
rejecting delayed fields and function values. An unknown enum variant
aborts the transaction, so no undecodable value is staged.

The natives are registered at 0x7 and the context is added to the Move
unit-test hook. The session does not register or drain the context
yet; with NATIVE_ORDERBOOK off the natives abort before reaching it.

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit adds a new native order book module and registers related natives; it introduces new functionality rather than correcting existing incorrect behavior.

subject: [vm] Freeze gas version 54 as released; 1.50 becomes 55
body:
* [vm] Freeze gas version 54 as released; 1.50 becomes 55

The testnet V2 reset (2026-10-06) went live with gas feature version 54:
its genesis was generated with a main-based CLI whose
LATEST_GAS_FEATURE_VERSION was RELEASE_V1_50 = 54, while the framework
came from this branch. Testnet has executed at 54 ever since, with the
seven keys every 1.49.x binary gates at RELEASE_V1_50. The hotfixes for
captured-value and captured-layout metering then added two more keys under the same version, so 1.49.7
nodes fail at VM startup on testnet with "Gas parameter
misc.abs_val.closure_per_captured_layout_byte does not exist. Feature
version: 54."

A version that is on chain is immutable: nodes take the version from the
on-chain GasScheduleV2, not from the binary. So rename 54 to
TESTNET_RESET_OCT_2026 and freeze it to exactly the seven genesis keys,
and make RELEASE_V1_50 = 55. Everything added after the genesis stays
gated at RELEASE_V1_50: the two hotfix parameters, the captured-layout
term of closure_abstract_size, the pack_closure charge in the meter and
meter_closure_captured_layouts. Everything the 1.49.3-1.49.6 binaries
ran at 54 moves to the new constant: closure_v2 and the type-argument
term, meter_closure_ty_args, the string and object natives. Mainnet
stays at 53 and LATEST_GAS_FEATURE_VERSION stays RELEASE_V1_49.

subject: [framework] Add hot state on-chain config
body:
Hot state parameters affect the hot state root, so they have to agree across
validators, yet today they are hardcoded or come from local node config. This
adds `0x1::hot_state_config` so they can be governed on chain. Nothing reads
it yet; that will follow once this ships in a framework release.

Like `execution_config`, the Move resource holds opaque BCS bytes of a
versioned Rust enum (`OnChainHotStateConfig`), so later fields only need a new
variant on the Rust side, without another framework release. `V1` has:

- `max_items_per_shard` (per shard, so currently 16 entries)
- `max_value_bytes_per_shard`: item count alone doesn't bound memory since
  value sizes vary widely
- `refresh_interval_versions`
- `max_promotions_per_block`

`initialize` is genesis-only, so on existing chains the config can only take
effect at an epoch boundary via `set_for_next_epoch`.

subject: [mono-move] Function reflection (#20628)
body:
Implements `0x1::reflect::native_resolve`, the AIP-133 function reflection
native, with the legacy VM's five error codes.

Resolution loads the target module once, priced into the read set, reads its
declared signature, and matches it against the caller-supplied function type to
infer the type arguments. The function itself is never loaded: the result is a
non-capturing closure holding `ClosureFuncRef::Unresolved`, which the existing
`CallClosure` path resolves and memoizes on first call.

Monomorphization plus canonical interning makes matching cheap. Identical
pointers mean identical subtrees, so a ground subtree settles in one compare and
a non-generic target costs two.

Natives reach the loader through one erased `LoaderAccess` trait object, which
replaces the `resource_group_of` closure the native context held. A trait object
is needed because `ProductionNativeContext` has a single lifetime parameter and
`&mut ModuleReadSet<'guard>` is invariant in `'guard`.

The differential harness seeded no `Features` resource, so
`is_function_reflection_enabled` was false and `resolve`'s assert would have
aborted identically on both VMs. Both harnesses now seed it from
`Features::default_for_tests`.

`reflect_typaram_reference.masm` stays in failing.toml: both VMs agree on the
abort code and location, and only the `AbortInfo` decoration differs, which is
the gap already tracked in the transaction executor's e2e tests.

subject: [storage] Apply the on-chain hot state config
body:
The hot state's item and byte caps and its refresh interval affect the hot
state root, so validators have to agree on them, yet they come from the local
node config.

Use `0x1::hot_state_config::HotStateConfig` once it exists on chain. Nothing
has set it yet, so the local config remains the fallback while it's absent.

Validators can't skip a block they fail to apply, so an invalid config would
halt the chain. `set_for_next_epoch` and `initialize` validate the config
through a native instead, making a bad governance proposal abort, and nodes
panic on an invalid config as a bug. The native isn't metered, like
`consensus_config::validator_txn_enabled_internal`, since only the framework
signer can reach it.

`State` now carries an `EffectiveHotStateConfig`. `State::update` looks for
writes to the config resource and applies each at its own version: the
eviction at that version already uses the new caps, so a reconfig that
shrinks the hot state evicts the excess in the reconfig txn itself, while the
new refresh interval applies to later updates, i.e. from the next epoch. Tying
this to versions keeps the result independent of how write sets are split into
chunks, e.g. when replaying several epochs on restart.

On startup the config is read at the latest snapshot version, which covers
restarts, fast sync and the db tools.

`delete_on_restart` stays local.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit adds validation of the on-chain hot state configuration and applies it safely, fixing a bug where an invalid config could cause a chain halt (panic). This addresses an availability issue that could be exploited via a malicious governance proposal, making it a security-relevant fix.

Previously these functions could be called by unauthorized parties, enabling an attacker to seize ownership or execute privileged calls, which is a classic improper access control vulnerability.

subject: [Functions] Separate event for invalid IDs (#8652)
body:
Emitting UserCallbackRawError when request ID was invalid had several issues:
1. It's not a user error - our contracts set the IDs.
2. OCR can sometimes send the same report twice (expected behavior). If we emit UserCallbackRawError on the second attempt, we cause observability issues (e.g. latency is calculated based on the last one instead of the first one).
3. Similarly - emitting this event causes seom problems in core node state transitions (unwanted and confusing error logs).

Apart from new event, I also cloned old interfaces into the testing dir, to avoid migrating changes in the future.
rationale: The change fixes incorrect handling of invalid request IDs by returning a specific enum and emitting a dedicated InvalidRequestID event instead of the generic UserCallbackRawError, addressing observability and node state issues. This corrects buggy behavior but does not introduce or mitigate a security vulnerability.

* Parallelize getUpkeepInfo (#9600)

Parallelize how we fetch upkeep information:

Extract a getUpkeepInfo function
Update getUpkeepInfo to accept a channel of uint16
Run 5 separate instances of getUpkeepInfo that each read from the same channel
Feed the channel with all the upkeep IDs we want to fetch info for
When getUpkeepInfo completes, send the info result into a results channel
When all the ids have been sent, close the id channel
This will cause each instance of getUpkeepInfo to terminate their loops and return
This unblocks the wait group
Read from the results channel and use the upkeep info as needed

subject: Token pool refactor (#453)
body:
## Motivation
Currently, token pools have to allow each individual onRamp and offRamp.
This means that when a lane gets upgraded, many new approvals need to be
given. With this new change, pools simply allowList a chain, and get the
correct ramp information via the Router. This gives an additional
security benefit of the router being the source of truth for supported
lanes, and any removal from the router will cut off the old lane from
token pool access as well.
rationale: The refactor adds a chain allow‑list check via the Router, introducing validation that previously was missing (evidenced by new tests like `testChainNotAllowedReverts`). This fixes an access‑control bug that could let unauthorized ramps interact with token pools, a potential fund‑loss vulnerability.

subject: fix(contracts): inline isContract() call in EVM2EVMOffRamp (#471)
body:
## Motivation
Compiling the `EVM2EVMOffRamp` token implementation for
[TVM](https://developers.tron.network/v3.7/docs/virtual-machine-introduction)
fails with the following error:

```
TypeError: Member "isContract" not unique after argument-dependent lookup in address.
--> github/smartcontractkit/ccip/contracts/src/v0.8/ccip/offRamp/EVM2EVMOffRamp.sol:438:8:
    |
438 | !message.receiver.isContract() || !message.receiver.supportsInterface(type(IAny2EVMMessageReceiver).interfaceId)
    | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

See https://github.com/tronprotocol/tronbox/issues/136 for more details.

## Solution

This change inlines the isContract() call to avoid ambiguity. Open
Zeppelin solves this issue similarly (see
https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/pull/3945/files).
rationale: The commit replaces a failing OpenZeppelin `isContract()` call with an inline `address.code.length == 0` check to fix a compilation error on TVM. This restores buildability but does not alter runtime logic, so it is a bug fix (compilation issue) without security impact.

subject: [lock/unlock] feat: arb L1<->L2 bridge plugin support (#490)
body:
This PR implements off-chain bridging support for Arbitrum and for the
Mock Bridge being used in the integration tests. In order to properly
test this logic in the integration tests a lot of changes unfortunately
had to be made and this PR is quite big. This description aims to
summarize the changes on each part of the rebalancer codebase so far.

## Bridges
"Bridging support" in the context of the rebalancer plugin involves
mainly two things as of time of writing (and may potentially involve
more things in the future as we develop this plugin):

1. Determining transfer state: The plugin needs to know the state of
each pending transfer that was initiated using a bridge. Certain states
allow the plugin to perform certain actions. For example, a pending
transfer in the state "finalized" means that the plugin can instruct the
Rebalancer contract onchain to inject liquidity into the attached
liquidity container.
2. Determining bridge-specific arguments: Each "side" of the bridge
involves using different sets of arguments for many bridges, and
therefore bridges are directional - e.g L1 -> L2 and L2 -> L1 are
different bridge implementations. For example, for the L2 -> L1
direction, the bridge-specific arguments determined for finalizing
withdrawals on L1 are fundamentally different than finalizing transfers
in the L1 -> L2 direction.

The `Bridge` interface in
`core/services/ocr2/plugins/rebalancer/bridge/bridge.go` is the
interface that will be implemented for all bridge directions and chains
supported. See the interface for the exact methods, which have
descriptive comments.

### Arbitrum L1 <-> L2 Bridge Implementations

In this PR, the `Bridge` interface referenced above is implemented for
both directions of the Arbitrum One bridge, L1 -> L2 and L2 -> L1. Their
contents are mostly based off of the scripts merged in #480, so in
essence there is not much new here other than rejigging some things in
order to be able to properly implement the logic housed in those
scripts.

## Graphs and Discovery

Discovery of the graph of liquidities was tightly coupled to the EVM
implementation of the `Rebalancer` interface in the `liquiditymanager`
package, and this was causing issues for initializing the bridges, since
they also need to know a lot of information about the graph as well,
mainly the rebalancer and bridge adapter contract addresses.

As such, this PR factors out the discovery from `liquiditymanager` into
a new `discoverer` package. This package provides the `Discoverer`
interface which is able to discover rebalancers starting from a
master/root/main rebalancer contract and network.

Right now only an EVM implementation is provided, which will be
sufficient for our needs, but can be expanded in the future if there are
non-EVM rebalancers.

The `liquiditygraph` package was renamed to `graph` since it is now
housing much more than just liquidity data:

```golang
type XChainRebalancerData struct {
	RemoteRebalancerAddress   models.Address
	LocalBridgeAdapterAddress models.Address
	RemoteTokenAddress        models.Address
}

type Data struct {
	Liquidity         *big.Int
	TokenAddress      models.Address
	RebalancerAddress models.Address
	XChainRebalancers map[models.NetworkSelector]XChainRebalancerData
}
```

The data housed now closely mirrors what is on-chain, since pretty much
all of. this is needed in the off-chain components (e.g bridge
implementations).

## Rebalancing Algorithms

The `random` and `dummy` algorithms have been deleted to ease
maintenance burdens and only `pingpong` is now available and used within
tests.

## Plugin Logic

Plugin logic has been changed in order to account for fetching
bridge-specific data. The phases now operate as follows:

1. `Observation`: the plugin syncs the rebalancer graph, by doing a
discovery and updating the liquidities on each rebalancer. This behavior
was there before and is unchanged. *Additional behavior*: we check the
previous outcome and check if there are any _proposed transfers_ from
the committed outcome. These outcomes are then _resolved_ by using the
bridge implementations. See `resolveProposedTransfers` in
`core/services/ocr2/plugins/rebalancer/plugin.go` for more details.
2. `Outcome`: the plugin constructs an outcome by: (a) computing median
liquidity per-chain (b) computing the consensus graph of connections
between chains (c) consensus on pending transfers. This behavior was
there before and is unchanged. *Additional behavior*: we compute a
quorum on the _resolved transfers_ that have been sent as part of the
observation. This is similar to the pending transfers consensus but
involves a little more details. See `computeResolvedTransfersQuorum` in
`core/services/ocr2/plugins/rebalancer/plugin.go` for details.
3. `Reports`: the previous plugin logic here was actually buggy. In
order to make it clearer what this function is supposed to do the code
now determines _incoming_ and _outgoing_ transfers for each network.
_Incoming_ transfers are transfers that are meant to generate `Receive`
instructions in the report, and _outgoing_ transfers are transfers that
are meant to generate `Send` instructions in the report. See `Reports`
in `core/services/ocr2/plugins/rebalancer/plugin.go` for more details on
this.
4. `ShouldTransmitAcceptedReport`: check the sequence number that has
been transmitted onchain and compare it to the provided `seqNr`. If
`onchainSeqNr < seqNrArg` then we return `true`, otherwise we return
`false`.

body:
## Motivation

The Optimism L1 bridge adapter needs to be able to both prove
withdrawals and finalize them on L1.

## Solution

* Add Optimism withdrawal proving and finalization on L1 functionality
to the bridge adapter. Tweak the scripts to prove and finalize
withdrawals through the adapters rather than on the Optimism contracts
directly to prove that they work.
* Fix a bug with ETH cross-chain transfers, on both L1 and L2 adapters:
since Optimism transfers ETH rather than WETH cross-chain through their
native bridge, stuff ends up reverting when we call `withdraw` on the
WETH contract prior to bridging.
* Fix a bug where we were using `withdrawTo` without actually sending
the ETH along with the call. The Optimism contracts dependency we're
using isn't bedrock so the `withdrawTo` function signature did not have
`payable`. Instead we copy/paste the `withdrawTo` function signature
directly from
[`L2StandardBridge.sol`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/f707883038d527cbf1e9f8ea513fe33255deadbc/packages/contracts-bedrock/src/L2/L2StandardBridge.sol#L114-L122),

subject: Permissionless token pools (#652)
body:
This PR is mainly focussed on the CCIP side of self serve token pools.
Some additional contracts had to be written/changed, but in review,
please focus on the CCIP & token pool side of self serve, not on the
TokenAdminRegistry.

Considerations

- Token pools are now considered hostile
  - This goes for both in- and output
  - Source side
    - Call to `sourcePool.lockOrBurn` from the onRamp
- Does not strictly have to be through a callWithExactGas call, as CCIP
is not paying for gas used here
      - Same for return data bomb
      - It returns the destPool and optional extraData
- DestPool has to be checked for length to mitigate the risk of return
data bombs through this field
- Since the onRamp is EVM2EVM, we can assume the address is an
abi.encoded(address) and therefore 32 bytes
        - ExtraData is checked like it was before
  - Dest side
    - We used to make a call to `getToken`
- Since this would be a hostile call, and require the full
callWithExactGas protection, we opted to fold this getter into the
`releaseOrMint` call. This saves a significant amount of gas, and makes
sure we only have to do a single call to the hostile contract.
    - We call `releaseOrMint` on the `pool` provided on the source side
- The pool data is considered hostile, as it came from an untrusted
source
- We need to ensure the address is valid and it contains a contract
      - The releaseOrMint call was already done through callWithExactGas

This brings the number of onchain calls to token pools to 2 per
transferred token: one on the source chain and one on the destination.
This is the absolute minimum possible.


Reviews for this PR should focus on

- Hostile token pool interactions
  - DoS
  - Unusual reverts
  - Gas bombs
  - Return data bombs
- The changes to CCIP and their impact on the security and availability
of the protocol

Please do not focus on

- The TokenAdminRegistry, except for things that would impact the
changed CCIP design

was minted or released from the pool. Using this functionality, it is
possible to create token pools that support tokens with different
decimals on different chains. There are various ways to implement this,
for instance, using the token pool return data to encode the source
chain decimals or some shared decimal schema. A pool could also maintain
a full decimal mapping of all remote chains and do the calculations on
the remote chain.

pool. Since `_callWithExactGasSafeReturnData` already does this check,
we only have to catch it in `_trialExecute` to safely remove the
duplicated check.


Due to the optimization in the check, the PR reduces gas usage while
adding the token pool functionality

subject: Implement PriceRegistry price data feed fallback (#718)
body:
## Motivation
Currently, the Price Registry relies on periodic price updates on-chain,
which is expensive and grows significantly as the number of supported
tokens grow. Instead, we can utilise price data feeds when they are
available on chain to significantly save on gas costs.

## Solution
Add ability to set data feeds per-token for the owner, which are then
used if available instead of the price mapping.

* Assumption: once a feed is set - we no longer need the fixed price -
so it is removed for gas cost savings
* Assumption: the same staleness threshold can be used for both data
feeds + manual token mappings
* Assumption: the `_getTokenPriceFromDataFeed` values will not underflow
on division if excessDecimals exceeds 36
rationale: The change introduces a new price feed fallback feature for the PriceRegistry without correcting any previously incorrect behavior; therefore it is not a bug fix and does not address a security defect.

pool so it is able to validate the token is supported by the pool.

Passing in the token also enables creating a token pool which supports
multiple tokens. To ensure the correct destination token is minted, the
pool should return the source/dest token in the extraData. This can then
be read by the dest pool.

token. This reduces the odds of a misconfiguration and closes some
potential exploit pathways.

lockOrBurn and ReleaseOrMint.

Optimizations for the onRamp had to be lowered a bit due to the extra
arguments used.
rationale: The commit adds token validation (isSupportedToken) to lockOrBurn, fixing a missing check that could allow misconfiguration and token misuse, which is a security-relevant bug that could be exploited to steal or misallocate funds.

subject: MultiAggregateRateLimiter - validation based contract with OffRamp implementation (#916)
body:
## Motivation
Re-designs the usage of the aggregate rate limiter, with a focus on the
OffRamp. The main motivations are:

* reduction of contract size in the OffRamp (and in next PR - for the
OnRamp) - from 24.79KB to 20.32KB
* increased flexibility & decoupling for message validations, allowing
to perform more than just rate limit checks
* ability to more easily control opt-in validations, with an easy way to
globally disable them

## Solution
The solution consists of multiple parts:
* `IMessageValidator`: an interface for hook contracts that can be
plugged into OffRamps/OnRamps to validate messages. The validation
functions revert if the validation criteria are not met
* `MultiAggregateRateLimiter`: the `AggregateRateLimiter` contract, but
converted to support multiple chains, with rate-limit specific logic
pulled in from the OffRamp. The contract now implements the
`IMessageValidator` interface
* `MultiOffRamp`: allows configuring an optional `IMessageValidator`,
which can perform any validation (in this case, we could set it to a
`MultiAggregateRateLimiter` contract)
* (removed) ~~`RateLimiterNoEvents`: the `RateLimiter` library converted
to exclude events (since they should now be per-chain). It was not
converted to a `RateLimiterMultiChain` to maintain the simplicity of the
library (since it should only act as a token bucket)~~

### Design choices
* `validateIncomingMessage` does not batch messages. The reason for this
is:
* To preserve generic chain inputs `Any2EVM`. Passing a batch of
`Any2EVM` messages requires more complex refactoring since we only have
`EVM2EVM` messages, which only get converted in `executeSingleMessage`
* Batching multiple messages would mean that rate limiting could fail
all messages, as opposed to treating them as isolated messages and
succeeding a large batch (e.g. in the current approach, the rate limit
could fail 1 out of 3 messages, but the other 2 would succeed. In
batching, this would not be the case)
* The logic is more in line with the previous `releaseOrMint` logic,
which treats each message as a single isolated unit
* Note that the main drawback is the gas cost - we are making multiple
external calls in this case
* A single `MultiAggregateRateLimiter` / `IMessageValidator` contract
should be used by both the OnRamp and the OffRamp, ~~which means that
the rate limiting state is shared~~
* (this is now separated per-lane) ~~We do not make a distinction of
lane `src -> dest` and `dest -> src`~~
* **All** `IMessageValidator` get caught by the validations in the
ramps. The reason is simplicity - unexpected failures should not trigger
unexpected bubbling reverts, and with this approach we do not need to
handle each specific validation error
* The message validator is expected to be shared by all lanes in a
single multi-ramp contract

### Out of scope for this PR
* OnRamp handling and on-ramp specific configurations in
`MultiAggregateRateLimiter`
* Message batching `MultiARL` / `IMessageValidator` (passing an array
instead of a single message)
* Considerations on whether the `MultiARL` should be per-lane or global
* (the expected behaviour is to not reset the ARL state on lane
re-deployments) ~~Multi-ARL state resets on re-deployment for a lane~~

---------

Co-authored-by: Rens Rooimans <github@rensrooimans.nl>
rationale: The commit introduces new contracts and refactors existing ones (MultiAggregateRateLimiter, IMessageValidator, MultiOffRamp) without fixing previously incorrect behavior; it is a feature/architecture change, not a bug fix, and no security-relevant bug is addressed.

subject: Let tokens hop through the offRamp (#962)
body:
## Solution
To ensure the end user gets the exact tokens they expect, we add an
extra hop through a trusted contract. Since token pools will be
considered hostile in the self-serve world, they cannot be trusted to
release the correct number of tokens, or even the correct token.

The offRamp functions as the trusted "hop" for all token releases, which
means that unless the token itself is malicious and simply doesn't
transfer when the offRamp calls the function, it should either revert or
deliver the exact number of tokens.


Other changes

- The mock usdc messenger now properly sends USDC to the receiver
  - This validates the correct mint privileges are supplies
- The offchain test doesn't appear to pass in the correct receiver of
this USDC, so we had to supply the USDC pool with funds manually. This
is not a downgrade of the test: previously no tokens were emitted or
ever sent to the receiver. In the new scenario the receiver gets the
correct number of tokens.
rationale: The change routes token releases through a trusted offRamp to prevent hostile token pools from delivering incorrect amounts or wrong tokens, fixing a defect where malicious pools could steal or withhold funds, which is a security-relevant behavior.

subject: Add LM Optimism L1 to L2 bridge interface (#840)
body:
This PR adds the Optimism bridge interface for L1 to L2 transfers. Some
important things to note:
- The Optimism L1 bridge adapter increments a nonce with each transfer
and each time `sendERC20` is called. This nonce is included in multiple
events throughout the transfer's lifecycle and is how we "match" and
link events together to confirm they've reached the various states.
- The `GetTransfers()` function makes use of this nonce and implements
the matching logic to link these 3 events together and partition
transfers into categories:
- L1's LiquidityManager `LiquidityTransferred.bridgeReturnData`, which
should equal
- OP's StandardBridge event `ERC20BridgeFinalized.extraData` which
should equal
  - L2's LiquidityManager `LiquidityTransferred.bridgeSpecificData`
