* predict/pricing: compute SVI variance and d2 at higher precision so short-dated prices stay accurate (DBU-665) (#1166)

* predict/pricing: carry variance, sqrt(w) and d2 at u128/1e18 (DBU-665)

`compute_nd2` formed the SVI variance increment as `mul_down(b, inner)`,
truncating the sub-unit fraction to a whole 1e9 unit. A five-minute surface
carries a total variance of about ten raw units at that scale, so the discarded
fraction was a material share of it, always downward, and `d2` is ill-conditioned
in the variance (a `w^-3/2` factor). Measured against a first-principles
reference on real Block Scholes surfaces, worst-case relative price error was
1.12% at one minute and 3.28% at five — the dominant published cadence — against
0.27% daily. The UP price feeds entry price, the live NAV mark and liquidation
thresholds, so the bias was systematic rather than noise.

`b` and the wing term are both 1e9-scaled, so their u128 product IS the 1e18
variance increment and the truncation simply disappears; the integer square root
of a 1e18 value is its 1e9-scaled root, so `sqrt(w)` returns at the scale the
rest of the formula already uses. Log-moneyness, the SVI geometry, the
smile-slope correction and the normal primitives are untouched. `fixed_math`
exposes `sqrt_u128_down`, which already existed privately; nothing is removed.

Two guard changes travel with it, recorded as RP-20: the positive-variance check
now reads the true sign rather than a 1e9 truncation, so a surface with
`0 < w < 1e-9` prices instead of aborting, and `d2` saturates at |8| — past where
`normal_cdf` already saturates — instead of overflowing. Both only turn an abort
into a priced result on the mandatory flush path.

The generator's analytic error model drops the variance product's floor, and a
short-dated scenario joins the corpus: worst-case per-endpoint budget falls from
307,052 to 3,304 raw units over the same four scenarios.

Test fallout was not a re-pin. The fixtures encoded `Phi(0) = 0.5 exactly`, which
was true only because `total_var / 2` floored half a raw unit to zero — the
at-the-money digital is 499,993,690, and `pricing_exact_tests` was asserting a
value 6,308 units from true math. Every flow test that derives money from the
price now checks that price against a generated first-principles digital within
`normal_cdf`'s documented 21-unit budget, then composes exactly on top. Swapping
the reference back to the old 500,000,000 fails 36 tests, so the check catches
the class of defect this commit fixes.

deployed variance range — is opened as P-16.

subject: predict: make full-pool valuation resumable across PTBs (DBU-679)
body:
The full-pool flush valued every active market in one atomic PTB, so it was
bounded by Sui's object-runtime cached-objects limit (1,000 dynamic-field
children per transaction, cumulative across the whole PTB). `walk_linear` loads
one child per distinct strike tick, so the budget was a joint sum across all
active markets and a single market at ~982 nodes already aborted the flush,
freezing LP supply/withdraw pool-wide. Tracked as predeploy item C-1.

Split the flush into a cheap atomic snapshot stage and a resumable valuation
stage:

  start_pool_valuation -> snapshot_expiry_pricer x N -> seal_valuation_snapshot
    (one PTB; reads oracles only, walks no trees)
  value_expiry x N
    (any number of transactions; one market's tree per transaction)
  finish_flush

`PoolValuation` stops being a hot potato and lives on the `PoolVault`, so it
survives across transactions. Each market's `Pricer` is frozen during the
snapshot stage and drives both the mark and the sweep-vs-value branch, so the
valuation stage reads no oracle and no clock: the pool is marked at the snapshot
instant no matter how many transactions valuation spans. That is what preserves
the exact single-mark property (audit L10) that the previous atomicity gave for
free.

Two cross-transaction hazards the single-PTB shape made unreachable:

- Settlement could move a market off the branch it was frozen on, so
  `try_settle` now takes the valuation lock. This cannot deadlock against the
  flush: `snapshot_expiry_pricer` refuses an expired-unsettled market, and that
  abort reverts the whole atomic snapshot transaction.
- An abandoned flush would hold the lock — which gates the entire mutation
  surface — indefinitely. `abort_valuation` is permissionless past
  `max_valuation_window_ms`; `abort_valuation_privileged` is immediate on the
  lifecycle authority. Partial NAV is discarded, since frozen marks are only
  sound as a simultaneous set.

`EWrongPoolVault` and its test are gone: the valuation is now a field of the
vault it belongs to, so a wrong-vault finish is unrepresentable rather than
rejected at runtime.

Verified: predict builds --warnings-are-errors; 464/464 tests; predeploy
check.py clean.

It adds a valuation lock with a timeout (max_valuation_window_ms) and abort mechanisms, preventing indefinite lock‑holding and restoring availability, thus constituting a security fix.

subject: predict: weight the trading fee by the pool's directional inventory (DBU-627)
body:
The trading fee is symmetric in the pool's position: it charges the same
whether a trade adds to the vault's directional exposure or offsets it, so
the pool accumulates inventory at no price.

This adds Block Scholes' post-MVP inventory weight from `DeepBook: Confidence
Price Adjustment`, applied to Predict's existing fee:

    fee = unweighted_fee · (1 ± sensitivity · min(1, |aggregate| / depth))

Dearer when a trade deepens the pool's lean, cheaper when it offsets one, and
exactly the unweighted fee whenever the mechanism is off, the book ends flat,
or the trade is directionally neutral. Predict's existing base fee is already
BS's `max(0.02·sqrt(p(1-p)), 0.005)` exactly, so the weight composes with what
is there rather than replacing it.

The mid is untouched. Pricing, NAV, the LP flush mark, mint admission, and
liquidation all continue to read the oracle's fair mark, so a complementary
pair of ranges still costs exactly its payout before fees and inventory can
never move the admitted-leverage curve or push an order across its knockout.
An earlier draft of this work skewed the mid instead (#1156, closed); moving
the signal to the fee removes that entire class of interaction.

The weight reads two stored quantities and no oracle state:

- The directional aggregate: exact signed position lots, maintained by one
  owned evaluator at mint, live close, and liquidation. It reads only atoms
  that round-trip losslessly through the packed order id, so a removal
  subtracts bit-equal what the insert added and no surface movement between
  open and close leaves a residual. Weighting a STORED aggregate by the live
  surface is what drifted in the reverted #995/#999 attempts; any
  price-dependent weighting belongs at read time.
- A per-expiry capital snapshot (`max_expiry_allocation`) that normalises it,
  so the depth is derived rather than hand-set and an expiry funded with twice
  the capital absorbs twice the position before its fee moves as far.

Quotes read the POST-trade position, so the weight cannot be dodged by
sequencing: an order that overshoots from one lean into the opposite one pays
for the exposure it created rather than being rewarded for the one it cleared.

Bounded on both sides. `max_inventory_fee_sensitivity` is strictly below 1.0,
so a fully-offsetting trade still pays a positive fee — at 1.0 it would pay
zero and beyond it the vault would owe a rebate, which makes a round trip
profitable and is a drain rather than an inducement. A zero depth (an expiry
funded below one lot) saturates instead of dividing by zero.

Ships disabled (`inventory_fee_sensitivity = 0`): every trade pays exactly
today's fee. Whether leaning the fee on inventory improves LP outcomes wants
live flow to answer, which is also what BS says calibration needs. The
aggregate is maintained while disabled, so enabling a later expiry needs no
migration.

subject: predict: charge an admin-configurable fee on PLP supply and withdraw fills (DBU-688)
body:
Adds `plp_fee_rate` to `ProtocolConfig`: one protocol-wide rate in
FLOAT_SCALING, default 1%, admin-settable inside a hard 0..5% envelope.

The fee is charged on the DUSDC leg of every executed LP fill and retained by
the pool, so it accrues to remaining PLP holders rather than the protocol
reserve. On supply it is deducted from the escrowed DUSDC before shares are
priced, so only the net buys PLP and the full escrow still joins idle. On
withdraw it is withheld from the marked payout, so the requester receives the
net while the full escrowed PLP is burned. Rounding is up, to the pool (R2).

Request-time `min_plp_out` / `min_dusdc_out` limits are compared against the
post-fee result, so a limit bounds what the requester actually receives.
Refunded, cancelled, and still-queued requests are never charged.

The rate is read once per flush into the frozen `FlushMark`, so every fill in
one flush is charged the same rate, and the setter is valuation-locked so it
cannot shift midway through a flush.

The fee never enters the mark: the mark stays the exact pool-wide NAV used in
both directions and the charge is applied after it. That is what separates it
from the superseded uncertainty-band withdraw fee of the approximate-NAV
design, which distorted the mark itself.

Events: `SupplyFilled` / `WithdrawFilled` gain `fee_dusdc`, and
`FlushExecuted` gains the `fee_rate` the flush froze. Both are additive.

Whether the fee should ship enabled, and at what rate, is not settled — see
predeploy open item P-27, which carries the experiment plan and decision rule.
rationale: only non-code files changed

subject: predict: default the PLP fee to 20 bps and pin the flush's config wiring (DBU-688)

Two changes on top of the fee itself.

Default `plp_fee_rate` is 20 bps (2_000_000), not 1%. The envelope is unchanged
at 0..5%, and the drain tests keep charging an explicit 1% because they pin the

Adds `flush_freezes_the_configured_plp_fee_rate`, the missing coverage of the

catches both a missing read and a stale one. Restoring the hard-coded zero now
fails it.

Reading the frozen rate needs `vault_events::flush_executed_fee_rate`, a
`#[test_only]` event-fields reader following the existing propbook precedent —
the frozen rate is otherwise unobservable from Move.
rationale: The commit fixes a bug where the flush logic ignored the admin-configured PLP fee rate and used a hard‑coded zero, allowing fees to be bypassed. This could be exploited to avoid paying protocol fees, causing economic loss, thus a security‑relevant fix.

subject: predict: make LP request attempts admin-tunable, shipping at one attempt (DBU-680) (#1175)
body:
* predict: refund an LP request that misses its limit instead of holding the queue head (DBU-680)

A queued supply/withdraw request whose quote fell below its own min_output was
left at the head with an incremented miss count while the drain broke out of the
queue, refunding only on the third miss. RP-12 held that the three-attempt expiry
"bounds queue blockage" — but the bound is per request and requests compose, so
a queue pre-stuffed with minimum-sized requests carrying an unsatisfiable limit
delayed every later LP by 2N+1 flushes at the cost of gas alone.

The head is now popped and refunded on the miss with RequestCancelled.reason = 2,
and the drain continues in the same flush, so every head is resolved when it is
reached. A miss spends one unit of that queue's budget, exactly like a fill.

The withdraw queue's FIFO-until-idle-dry carry is a different mechanism and is
unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict: make LP request attempts admin-tunable, shipping at one (DBU-680)

At 1 the behaviour is what the previous commit shipped: a limit miss refunds at

subject: predict: fill LP supplies up to an admin-tunable pool-value cap, with partial fills on both queues (DBU-684) (#1184)
body:
* predict: cap LP-attributable pool value with an admin-tunable ceiling (DBU-681)

Adds ProtocolConfig.max_lp_pool_value, checked in the supply pass at the frozen
flush mark: a supply that would carry pool value past the ceiling is refunded
with RequestCancelled.reason = 3 and the drain continues. Defaults to u64::MAX,
so the pool is uncapped until an operator sets a figure.

The check runs against the frozen mark plus the supplies already filled this
flush, so a run of individually-fitting requests cannot collectively overshoot,
and it is evaluated before the user's own limit because no re-submitted limit can
make a full pool admit a deposit.

Caps pool value rather than cumulative deposits: no new running-total state, and
it bounds the quantity an operator wants bounded. The consequence, documented in
RP-23, is that trading profit alone can carry a capped pool above its ceiling,
after which supplies refund until NAV falls back. Withdrawals and issued PLP are
never gated, so a cap below current pool value closes the pool without trapping
anyone in it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict: pin that a full pool clears its supply queue rather than holding it (DBU-684)

A capped pool refunds every queued supply in the flush that reaches it — there is
no waiting list, which is the direct consequence of refusing to let an unfillable
head sit at the front. Pins that, and that the per-queue budget still bounds how
much of a full queue one flush clears.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict: pin a full capped flush end to end (DBU-684)

One flush with a binding cap across both queues: supplies drain first against the
frozen mark until headroom runs out, then withdrawals pay with no capacity check.
Pins the ordering consequence too — a request refused for capacity does not
reserve the room it wanted, so a smaller request queued behind it still fills.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict: partially fill a supply up to the cap, and address the stack review (DBU-684)

Partial fills, on Tony's call: a supply larger than the remaining headroom now takes
what fits and has the rest returned in the same transaction, instead of being
refunded whole. Headroom therefore follows queue order rather than going to whichever
later request happens to be small enough, and pool value lands exactly on the cap.

This required moving the limit check ahead of the capacity check. Pricing is linear
at a frozen mark, so "this prefix clears the LP's rate" is exactly the existing
shares >= min_output test on the full amount — no new arithmetic, and min_plp_out
becomes a price floor rather than an absolute share floor. Two floors bound the
prefix: min_supply_request, and a non-zero share quote.

From the independent review of the stack:
- The cap floor was short by min_supply_request, so a cap at the legal minimum left
  a bootstrapped pool with zero headroom forever — the doc claimed the opposite and
  a flow test demonstrated the falsehood while reading as success. Floor raised to
  genesis lock + one minimum supply, with an honest note that it is a sanity bound
  and not a liveness guarantee.
- Nothing asserted RequestCancelled.reason anywhere, so the branch order was
  unpinned. Added the two tests that distinguish reasons; mutation-checked by
  restoring the old cap-before-limit order, which now fails.
- RP-23 claimed the cap touches the supply pass only. Supplies fund same-flush
  withdrawals, so refusing them can push a large exit to a later flush; blast radius
  now says so.
- Both new admin knobs were missing from configuration.md.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict: partial fills hold their queue place, on both sides (DBU-684)

Supplies: a head larger than the remaining headroom is filled up to the cap and
its unfilled balance stays escrowed at the head, keeping position, index and
owner; the pass then breaks. A head with no room is left untouched and the pass
breaks without spending budget. Nothing is refunded for capacity, so the
capacity reason code is unreachable and removed.

Breaking forfeits no throughput — once the cap is reached nothing behind the head
could fill either — and it bounds per-flush drain work at O(1) under a binding
cap, which matters against the flush's event ceiling. A full pool now holds its
queue instead of clearing it every flush.

Withdrawals partially fill on the same principle: a head whose payout exceeds
idle is paid what idle covers and keeps the balance queued. Shares to burn are
floored from available idle and the payout is quoted from those shares by the
same helper a full fill uses, so a partial exit prices identically to a whole one
and the pool never releases cash it has not destroyed shares for.

A carried request keeps asking for the same price, so its min_output is scaled to
the remaining amount and rounded UP — at worst the requester is held to a
fractionally stricter limit, never a laxer one.

Also: a capacity break spends no flush budget, matching the withdraw pass; RP-2
updated for partial withdrawals; RP-23 rewritten.

subject: predict: pin the fee reported on supply and withdraw fill events
body:
The balance assertions cannot see a wrong `fee_dusdc`. Shares and cash both come
from the quote's `output`, so an event reporting the wrong fee leaves every
balance assertion green while misattributing pool revenue to off-chain
consumers, which is where the charge is accounted from.

Found by mutation: reporting the whole request's fee on a partially-filled
supply, instead of the filled slice's, passed all 513 tests. It now fails
`supply_fill_reports_the_fee_charged_on_the_slice`.

Adds `#[test_only]` fee readers for both fill events, following the existing
propbook precedent for event-field readers, and asserts the reported figure on a
partial supply fill — where the slice fee and the whole request's fee differ —
and on a withdrawal.
rationale: The diff only adds test-only getter functions and new tests; it does not modify the logic that emits fee values in events. No runtime behaviour is changed, so the commit does not correct a previously wrong behaviour.

subject: predict: fixes from the independent review of DBU-688
body:
Two public docs still told users the pool charges no LP-side fee, which is now
false at HEAD and was the review's only High-severity class:
- `docs/risks.md` — the bullet also built a safety argument on the absence of a
  fee ("safe precisely because the mark is exact"). Rewritten: the mark is still
  exact and still dual-use, and the charge sits outside it.
- `docs/design/invariants.md` — asserted "no fee" as an invariant.

RP-23's "at most one ulp of idle is left behind" is no longer true with a fee
set; the register now carries the actual bound (the slice's fee plus the ulp) and
why the second inversion was declined. The matching source comment said the same
stale thing and is fixed with it.

`fee_on` relies on the envelope keeping the rate below 1.0 for `amount - fee`
never to underflow inside the mandatory flush, and that guarantee lived only in a
comment. `plp_fee_rate_envelope_cannot_reach_full_scale` pins it, so widening the
envelope fails a test instead of aborting a live flush.

Two coverage gaps on the highest-risk paths, both mutation-checked:
- the idle-short withdraw branch was only ever exercised at zero fee, so the
  gross inversion and its retained-fee bound were untested;
- no supply test carried both a limit and a fee, where the per-slice ceil'd fee
  meets the pro-rated limit at its exact boundary.

`plp_fee_rate` narrowed from `public` to `public(package)`: `ProtocolConfig` is a
shared object, so off-chain callers read the field directly, which is why the
equally SDK-relevant `max_lp_pool_value` is not public either. The `#[test_only]`
event readers move out of the `public(package)` block to the module end.

P-27 records the review's economics finding: because the fee is retained by the
pool, a supplier immediately refunds a share of it equal to their post-fill
ownership, so the effective rate is `F * (1 - share)` and tends to zero for the
largest LP — the actor best placed to time the mark pays the least of the charge
meant to price that timing. Calibration has to target the effective rate.

subject: predict: fixes from the second independent review of DBU-688
body:
`liquidity-and-nav.md` still carried the pre-fee fill formulas. The earlier pass
edited that file's NAV-rework note but left the two formulas, both `min_*_out`
definitions, and the drain walkthrough describing a fee-free protocol — in the
file the other three docs point at for LP mechanics. An integrator sizing
`min_plp_out` from the documented formula would have been refunded every flush at
the shipped one-attempt setting.

P-27's worked example was arithmetically wrong: the holding is worth 9_989_989
and the net fee is 10_011, not 9_990_000 and 10_000. The identity it illustrates
(`F * (1 - post_fill_share)`) was right; only the numbers were not. Recorded the
closed form `F * V / (V + n - F)` alongside it so it can be rederived. (Note the
tempting `F * V / (V + n)` is NOT it — that drops the fee from the denominator
and understates the charge.)

"Accrues to the holders who stayed" was wrong on the supply leg: the payer is a
holder the instant the fill lands and immediately recaptures their post-fill
share, which is the whole point of the P-27 economics added in the same branch.
Corrected to pro-rata, with the withdraw leg still reading "stayed".

`plp_fee_rate_envelope_cannot_reach_full_scale` asserted two constants and called
nothing, which unit-tests Rule 5 names directly. Replaced with an
`expected_failure` that drives the real validator at full scale.

The parity oracle is marked, not patched. `python_replay.py` claimed "NO withdraw
fee" in two places and models a fee-free drain, so any parity run at a non-zero
rate mismatches by exactly the fee. It now says so, states that runs must stage
`plp_fee_rate = 0` until the fee is derived there independently, and explains why
mirroring the Move formula across would defeat the oracle. `sim.ts` normalizers
now carry `fee_dusdc` so a future fee-enabled run can gate it.

Also: RP-23's pinning list now names the two tests covering its amended bound,

subject: predict: harness probe for the trade-path liquidation-budget ceiling (DBU-695)
body:
`trade_liquidation_budget` bounds the ambient liquidation pass before every
mint and live redeem. It ships at 24 and is admin-raisable to a compile-time
max of 3,000 that no measurement stands behind, which is what Three Sigma
issue #48 asks about.

Adds the instrument, not the answer:

- `setTradeLiquidationBudgetTx` — the AdminCap-gated protocol_config setter.
- Keeper ladder `TRADE_LIQ_BUDGET_STAGES="<elapsedSeconds>:<budget>,…"`,
  applied one rung at a time and traced as {type:"liqBudget", budget}. The
  pass costs min(budget, active_leveraged_orders), so a book built cheaply at
  24 is re-probed at every higher rung without rebuilding it — one run sweeps
  the range. Unset leaves the contract default, so existing runs are unchanged.
- `KEEPER_LIQ_BUDGET` sizes the keeper's own liquidate() lane and takes 0 to
  disable it, so the adverse arm's liquidatable orders survive for a mint's
  ambient pass to meet.
- `liq-budget-sweep` (healthy: 1.1x, nothing knocks out, isolates scan+price)
  and `liq-budget-adverse` (near-ATM at the admission cap, so the pass meets
  liquidatable candidates and pays index + payout-tree removal).

Batching is adaptive because every mint in a PTB runs its own ambient pass:
the batch starts at 40 and halves on each OOG down to 1, and a 1-leg batch is
byte-identical to an ordinary mint, so every submission at batch==1 is itself
the measurement.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The change only introduces new prediction harness features and environment variables for measuring trade liquidation budget; it does not correct previously incorrect behavior, so it is not a bug fix nor a security fix.

subject: predict: split the PLP fee into independent supply and withdraw rates (DBU-688)
body:
Ships asymmetric: `plp_supply_fee_rate` at 0, `plp_withdraw_fee_rate` at 20 bps,
each in the same 0..5% envelope with its own setter and error code.

Entry is no longer taxed. An exit concentrates the pool's outstanding risk on
whoever stays — the written liabilities do not shrink when an LP leaves, so the
same risk sits on a smaller base — while a deposit dilutes it and is a benefit to
the pool's health. The charge that prices that externality therefore belongs on
the exit alone. The supply knob still exists so the decision is reversible
without a package upgrade, not because a supply charge is intended.

The flush event now reports the pair read OFF THE MARK rather than the config
locals. Found by mutation: handing `new_flush_mark` the supply rate for both
slots passed all 522 tests, because the withdraw leg cannot be driven
behaviourally from a Move test — a unit-test accumulator root carries no
settlement funds, so a fill's PLP never reaches custody to be withdrawn. At the
shipped defaults that mutation silently charges no withdraw fee at all, i.e.
disables the feature on the only leg that charges. `lp_book::fee_rates` makes the
mark the single source for what the event reports, and
`flush_freezes_both_configured_fee_rates` now fails on it.

Every drain test drives only the leg it exercises (`ONE_PERCENT_FEE, NO_FEE` or
`NO_FEE, ONE_PERCENT_FEE`) rather than setting both, so a quote reading the wrong
leg's rate is a detectable bug rather than an invisible one.

P-27 records the basis splitting in two: utilization-on-exit justifies a non-zero
exit fee with no calibration and no adversary, while model-estimation error is
the half that needs measuring — and sizing that against the ~1% certified
arithmetic bound is the wrong yardstick, since that bound is the pricer's
numerical envelope, not the vendor's model error. The economics note is rewritten
for the asymmetric shape: with supply at 0 the self-refund is live only on
partial exits, where a holder keeping most of their stake recaptures most of the
charge and a full exit pays it in full — the right direction, but it means the
effective rate is not the nominal one for large partial exits.
rationale: only non-code files changed

subject: predict: fixes from the third independent review of DBU-688
body:
The event↔mark coupling was a comment, not a guard. Reverting the event to read
the config locals instead of the mark changed no behaviour and left 522/523
green, silently restoring the invisibility the previous commit existed to remove.
The config reads are now inlined into `new_flush_mark`, so no local survives for
the event to report instead — the alternative source stops existing rather than
being warned about.

`fees-and-rebates.md` still explained the self-refund on the supply leg, which
now charges nothing, while P-27 explained it on partial exits. Same mechanism,
two documents, different legs. Rewritten for the leg that charges: a full exit
pays the fee in full, a partial exit pays `F * (1 - post_withdrawal_share)`.

P-27's economics had the direction backwards. The deviation from the nominal
rate is largest for the SMALLEST exits — recapture falls as the exit fraction
rises — not for "large partial exits" as written. It also grafted the new
analysis onto the old supply-leg worked example so the conclusion no longer
followed. Rewritten, with the example kept as the dormant symmetric analogue.

Recorded what the split does to the item's own measurement: a round trip now
costs `F_out` alone rather than `F_in * (1 - share) + F_out`, so the timing loop
pays a flat 20 bps instead of the ~40 a symmetric rate would have charged a small
LP. The experiment has to be read against that figure.

Also: `max_withdraw_fee_rate_withholds_five_percent` drives the envelope ceiling
on the leg that is actually live (it was only covered on the supply side), the
full-scale rejection test is named for the leg it drives, and the last two stale
`plp_fee_rate` references are gone.
rationale: only non-code files changed

subject: predict: derive the ambient-pass cost curve in analyze (DBU-695)
body:
The probe's trace was raw JSONL nobody joined. This turns it into the
deliverable: join the keeper's budget rungs to each single-mint probe, fit
comp ~ base + slope*candidates, and report the per-candidate cost, the mint's
own base, and the candidate count at which an ordinary mint stops fitting one
tx — which is the number max_trade_liquidation_budget gets set under.

Fit notes, both load-bearing:
- Regress on candidates = min(budget, book), not budget. Below saturation the
  book is what the pass actually walks, so fitting on budget understates the
  slope.
- Use only n==1 batches. A 1-leg batch is byte-identical to an ordinary mint,
  while an N-mint PTB pays N ambient passes and would flatten the slope.

With no ladder configured the section is skipped rather than assuming the
contract default, so ordinary runs print exactly what they printed before.

Tests synthesise a trace from a known cost model and assert the fit recovers
it, with expectations hand-computed as literals rather than re-derived with
the fit's own formula. Both fixtures are shaped to bite: one rung is
book-limited (so regressing on budget gives a different answer) and one rung
carries a real multi-mint batch (so dropping the n==1 filter collapses the
slope). Mutation-checked — reverting either fit decision fails 2 tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit adds new analysis code and tests for deriving a cost curve; it does not modify existing behavior to correct a defect, nor does it address any security-relevant issue.

subject: predict: conform the fee surface to the Sui Move conventions
body:
Audited the branch against Sui's Move best-practices checklist. Two changes.

`lp_book::fee_rates` returning `(u64, u64)` becomes `supply_fee_rate` and
`withdraw_fee_rate`. The checklist names `property_name` as the convention for
field access, and per-leg reads also remove the transposition risk the pair
carried at its one call site — the emitted rate is now named where it is read,
not positional.

`new_flush_mark` gains a doc comment stating its argument order. It is now a run
of four same-typed `u64`s, which `predict-contracts.md` warns about and which is
the shape that produced the swapped-rate mutation this branch already had to
close.

Verified conformant, no change needed: struct ability order (`copy, drop` on
`FillQuote`), error constants as PascalCase `E*`, test constants as
UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, the `// === Test-Only Functions ===` section header against
five in-repo precedents, admin capability as the second setter parameter,
imports grouped by dependency source, and doc comments on the public surface —
the package-only config getters and `assert_*` helpers are left undocumented
deliberately, matching both their siblings and the repo rule exempting plain
package config accessors.

Not adopted: the checklist's `Event` suffix for event structs. `SupplyFilled` /
`WithdrawFilled` / `FlushExecuted` predate this branch and renaming them is an
event-schema break for off-chain consumers, unrelated to the fee.
rationale: The change only refactors a tuple-returning function into two separate getters and updates the call site accordingly. No functional behavior or security-relevant logic is altered, indicating a naming/convention improvement rather than a bug fix.

subject: predict: only the adverse arm declares the wall, and stop probing once it is measured (DBU-695)
body:
Two problems from a self-review of the previous commits.

Both arms declared `InsufficientGas`, but at the pre-memo correction_value
slope a scan-only pass at the 3,000 budget max costs ~73% of the computation
cap — it fits. So the healthy arm was declaring a wall it is not expected to
reach, which fails every clean run VACUOUS, and worse, would have whitelisted
the OOG if it ever did happen. A scan-only mint that cannot fit is a bigger
finding than the one being measured and belongs to the bug oracle. The
declaration is now per-arm and only liq-budget-adverse carries it.

At batch==1 an OOG left nothing to halve, so the probe re-submitted a failing
~cap-sized tx every tick forever: an OOG still executes and charges, so the
trader's gas coin drains and the trace fills with duplicate wall records.
The wall is now confirmed three times and then the strategy holds; any
success resets the counter.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The change stops an infinite OOG loop that previously drained the trader's gas coin and filled the trace with duplicate wall records, fixing a resource‑exhaustion bug that could be triggered to cause denial‑of‑service and financial loss.

subject: predict: reset probe state on market re-lock (DBU-695)
body:
Found by enumerating the strategy's state across failure boundaries, which
the repo's review rules require for stateful async code.

`targetMarket` reset `minted` when the locked market settled but carried
`batch` and `wallHits` into the new one. A run that had reached the wall
re-locks at batch==1 with wallHits already past its limit, so the hold
triggers immediately and the strategy never mints into the fresh empty book —
it idles for the rest of the run. All book-derived state now resets together.

Also documents the keeper ladder's restart behaviour: it is in-memory, so a
restart replays from the first rung and walks the budget back down before
climbing. That costs run time, not correctness — rungs are traced and each
probe joins to the rung in force at its own timestamp.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The change resets `batch` and `wallHits` to their initial values when the locked market changes, fixing a logic error where stale state prevented the strategy from minting after a market re‑lock.

subject: predict: keep the hot potato for the snapshot stage, and close the review findings (DBU-679)
body:
Review of the resumable-valuation change found that dropping PoolValuation's hot
potato gave up more than the resumable stage needed. The valuation stage had to
lose it; the snapshot stage did not, and its atomicity is the entire correctness
argument for the frozen mark.

- start_pool_valuation returns a SnapshotStage potato, snapshot_expiry_pricer
  borrows it, seal_valuation_snapshot consumes it. One-transaction snapshot is now
  a property of the type system rather than a keeper convention, and the otherwise
  permissionless stage is scoped to whoever started the flush.
  EValuationSnapshotSealed is deleted: the potato makes it unreachable.
- max_valuation_window_ms moves from a compiled constant to a bounded AdminCap
  setter (5 min - 4 h, default 1 h). It decides the maximum protocol pause a
  stalled keeper can cause, which is an operator decision tuned against flush
  cadence, and the setter refuses to move under a flush in flight.
- Harness updated to the staged API: keeperFlushTxs returns the snapshot PTB, one
  value_expiry transaction per market, then finish; the keeper discards a stranded
  valuation on failure. treeNodeSweep.ts, which C-4 needs, works again.
- Coverage for what the potato used to guarantee: both abort paths, the deadline
  pinned from both sides, the try_settle gate, double-snapshot, expired-unsettled
  snapshot, the window's bounds, and the flush's inherited same-transaction oracle
  refusal.
- Docs: eight sites still described the removed potato, three in live source
  docstrings including the module that owns the lock. Corrected, along with the
  risks.md bullet that listed cancellations as blocked and then called escrow
  cancellable throughout, and the external-audit issue references that resolved
  publicly to an unrelated PR.

Verified: build --warnings-are-errors clean, predict 523/523, check.py clean,
format-move clean, harness tsc clean. Mutation-checked: collapsing the abort
deadline fails only permissionless_abort_before_the_deadline_aborts, and removing
the try_settle gate fails only settling_during_a_flush_aborts.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: [MEV] The change restores the atomic snapshot stage by keeping the hot‑potato token, fixing a bug where the snapshot could be taken out of order. The prior lack of atomicity could allow an attacker to manipulate valuation ordering and produce incorrect pool NAV, a financial loss vector, thus a security‑relevant race condition.

subject: predict: fix the probe so it actually measures anything (DBU-695)
body:
From the independent review. The instrument, run exactly as its own README
documented, collected ZERO measurements and then printed an affirmative
"affordable" verdict — the worst possible outcome for a measurement tool.

Batching to the index cap saturated the book in ~3 minutes, long before the
first ladder rung at 900s. After that `MAX_BOOK - minted` was zero, no mints
were submitted, and the remaining rungs went unprobed. The "hold; the ladder
keeps re-probing" comment was simply false: a mint is the only probe.
Compounding it, `batch` halved only on OOG and never recovered, so it settled
at whatever fitted and n==1 records — the only ones the fit uses — appeared at
the top rung if at all.

Fixes:

- Fill to FILL_TARGET (2,000) with batches, then send every mint alone for the
  rest of the run. 3,000 single mints of headroom, ~75 min, outlasting the
  documented ladder. Verified by driving the real strategy module against a
  modelled contract: 2,350 single-mint probes spread 250/300/300/300 across
  all four rungs, against zero before.
- Track the ACTIVE index (mints issued minus OrderLiquidated events from each
  tx) and trace it as `book`; `analyze` fits against that. On the adverse arm
  the ambient pass removes orders continuously, so issued-mints overstated the
  candidates scanned, understating the slope and overstating the ceiling — the
  unsafe direction, on the arm the audit issue is actually about.
- Bracket each rung with `requestedAtMs`; `analyze` discards probes inside the
  request-to-landed window instead of crediting them to the older, lower rung
  (measured: up to -14% on the slope, +6% on the ceiling).
- Raise `liq-budget-wall-undeclared` when a single mint OOGs on an arm that
  never declared that wall. The OOG is traced as a mintBatch record, not a
  `fail`, so the bug oracle could not see it and the run exited 0 — which made
  liqBudgetSweep's own doc claim untrue.
- Give up loudly after 3 consecutive rung failures rather than retrying a
  doomed rung all run: `protocol_config` is a GUARD module, so the repeated
  aborts classified as expected and the run swept nothing yet exited 0.
- `||` not `??` for both env knobs — `KEEPER_LIQ_BUDGET=` coerced to 0n and
  silently disabled the keeper's liquidation lane.

Tests: 5 new cases covering the wall's smallest-candidate rule, multi-leg OOGs
not counting as the wall, book-vs-minted, and the undeclared-wall signal.
Mutation battery of 8 targeted mutants, all killed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit fixes a bug where the probe collected zero measurements and incorrectly reported affordability, which could mislead users into executing unaffordable transactions and lose funds. The changes add proper tracking, OOG detection, and signaling, correcting the unsafe behavior.

subject: predict: derive the payout-tree cap from the per-transaction object budget (DBU-679)
body:
Closes the single-market case RP-25 left open. RP-25 removed the joint budget
across markets but left the per-market one at a number that could not fit:
max_payout_tree_nodes was 1,000, equal to the whole 1,000-child transaction
budget, before ceil(5,000/64) = 79 liquidation pages and the market's base
children. A market filled to the cap was therefore permanently un-valuable, and
finish_flush requires every snapshotted market valued — so one such market froze
LP supply and withdraw pool-wide, for the price of the fees.

max_payout_tree_nodes is now derived rather than chosen:

    object_cache_budget - max_liquidation_pages - valuation_base_children_reserve
    = 1,000 - 79 - 40 = 881

Deriving it rather than picking a smaller literal is the point: raising
max_active_leveraged_orders now shrinks the node cap automatically instead of
silently pushing the flush back over the ceiling. valuation_capacity_tests.move
pins the arithmetic, and sui move test does not enforce the object-runtime limit,
which is exactly why it is asserted as arithmetic rather than left to a localnet
run nobody repeats.

Accepted cost: ~12% fewer distinct strike boundaries per market (1,000 -> 881),
which tightens wide-strike books. Correctness wins because the failure mode is a
pool-wide LP freeze, not a narrower grid.

The reserve is UNMEASURED and deliberately generous — source inspection puts the
real base under 10, the C-1 campaign implies ~18 in a fuller PTB. C-4 narrows to
tightening it; the unsafe case it used to guard is now unrepresentable.

Verified: build --warnings-are-errors clean, predict 526/526, check.py clean,
format-move clean. Mutation-checked: restoring the old literal 1_000 fails all
three capacity tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: only non-code files changed

subject: predict: fix the verdict layer, which was wrong in both directions (DBU-695)
body:
Second independent review. The arithmetic was sound; the pass/fail layer on
top of it was not.

1. The adverse arm reported VACUOUS even when it reached the wall it declared.
   The declared-wall check reads failed-tx artifacts and `fail` records; the
   trader submits via signExecThreaded, which writes no artifact (unlike the
   keeper's executeAndWait), and the probe traces its OOG as a mintBatch
   record. So neither source could ever see it and `reached` was always empty
   — the report printed the wall and "never reached" two lines apart. The
   OOG's own tag is now carried forward as the evidence.

2. A run that collected nothing printed an affirmative "affordable" line and
   exited 0, and a run whose samples clustered in a narrow band printed a
   ceiling extrapolated ~75x from it — 2.4x off truth, with an unphysical
   negative base mint, to the same decimal places as a real measurement. Now:
   no samples is its own signal, the fit demands a 4x lever arm, a negative
   base is refused outright, and a crossing far past the measured range is
   labelled extrapolation.

3. A rung failing 3x threw from applyBudgetStages, which runs before tick()
   inside the same try, with a counter that never cleared — so settlement,
   flush, rebalance and roll never ran again for the rest of the run. One bad
   rung bricked every other keeper lane, against the harness's own per-step
   isolation invariant. It now abandons the ladder and marks the trace fatal,
   which fails the run in analyze without touching the other lanes.

Also: only re-lock (and reset the book counter) on a genuinely DIFFERENT
market — markets() returns [] on a torn read, and treating that as "settled"
left the traced book under-reporting the live index for the rest of the run;
carry per-tx `knocked` so the adverse arm's removal cost is separable from
scan cost; and correct 73% -> 65% of the computation cap at budget 3,000
(the 73% figure assumed a 400M base mint against a measured ~2M).

Verified end-to-end: real strategy module driven against a modelled contract
for a full 3,600s ladder, trace fed to the real analysis — slope 1,086,000,
base 2,000,000, crossing 4,602, all exact; 65% of cap at budget 3,000; no
signals. A simulated markets.json blip now leaves zero book drift. 37 tests,
12 targeted mutants all killed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit corrects incorrect analysis logic in the predict harness (fit handling, negative base mint rejection, extrapolation warnings, and wall tag handling). This changes behavior that was previously wrong, qualifying it as a bug fix, but the changes affect only offline analysis tooling and do not introduce or mitigate any security-relevant vulnerability.

subject: predict: close the flush-hijack hole and fix the page-count bound (DBU-679)
body:
Two independent fresh-context reviews of the previous commits found defects the
author's own pass missed. Both are fixed here.

1. The hot potato was carrying a FOURTH duty nobody inventoried: authorization.
   On main, finish_flush consumed a PoolValuation only start_pool_valuation could
   mint, so only the flush starter could complete a flush. Moving the valuation
   onto the vault made value_expiry and finish_flush reachable by anyone, and a
   third party finishing with zero drain budgets retires the frozen mark with no
   LP request filled - under_budget(Some(0), 0) is 0 < 0 = false - forcing the
   operator to re-value the whole pool. One cheap transaction, repeatable every
   flush. PoolValuation now records started_by and both entrypoints assert it.
   There is deliberately no permissionless completion path: an abandoned flush is
   discarded by abort_valuation, not finished by a stranger.

2. max_liquidation_pages divided by the page capacity (64), which is the best
   case, not the bound. insert_active_order_id splits an over-full page at its
   midpoint - 32 and 33, never 64 - and merge_page_if_small declines exactly when
   the neighbour is full, so ascending order ids leave every page at the split
   floor. The real bound is ceil(orders / 32) = 157 pages, not 79, and the
   derived cap of 881 still overshot the budget. Now 1,000 - 157 - 40 = 803.
   The page capacity is single-homed in constants and liquidation_book reads it.

The capacity tests were tautologies - each reduced to budget <= budget once the
macro was substituted, and all three stayed green through the factor-of-two error.
Replaced with a structural test that builds a real book in ascending-id order and
counts real pages against the derivation's own occupancy assumption, plus a floor
assertion, since a derived cap can be driven to a positive but dead value without
underflowing. Mutation-checked: reverting the divisor fails the occupancy test.

RP-26 corrected: rung 2 not rung 3 (nothing stops a caller batching two
value_expiry commands into one PTB), MEASURED downgraded to the 1,000-child budget
alone, and the ~18 base-children figure retracted - the evidence bounds a
fuller-PTB overhead to [19, 292] and is not per-market at all; source inspection

subject: predict: bound payout-tree depth against caller-chosen strike ticks (DBU-693) (#1191)
body:
* predict: balance the payout tree by height, not by a hash of the tick

strike_payout_tree was a treap whose rotation priority was
blake2b256(bcs(tick)) — a pure function of a caller-chosen boundary, with
no salt and no market identity. A treap's shape depends only on its
{tick, priority} set, not arrival order, so a caller could scan for ticks
whose priorities descend as the ticks ascend and force a right spine.

The mint-time grid does not prevent this. assert_admitted_mint_ticks
requires each boundary to be a multiple of admission_tick_size / tick_size
(or the market's reference_tick), but at a 10x multiple that still leaves
~1.07e8 admissible boundaries, and a full 1,000-tick descending chain is
found in ~0.6s of laptop CPU. The fixture in the new test is entirely
on-grid: 100 such ticks built a depth-100 linked list where 100 honest
on-grid ticks built depth 13. At the 1,000-node cap a single mint would
touch 1,001 dynamic-field children against Sui's 1,000-per-transaction
ceiling, and the skew did not self-heal — honest mints attached around the
chain rather than breaking it up. External audit issue #47.

Rotations now key on measured subtree height (AVL), which nothing outside
the tree can choose, so depth is O(log n) for every tick set rather than in
expectation over a random one. The same adversarial fixture now builds
height 7, identical to the honest book.

No value changes. combine_summaries is an associative max-prefix-sum fold
over the in-order sequence and walk_linear rounds per node before any
structure is involved, so re-parenthesising the fold is a no-op on every
output: all 463 pre-existing tests pass unmodified, including both
metamorphic GC tests and the ascending-memo guard in payout_tree_walk_tests.

apply_at gets shorter — the two inline rotation branches collapse into one
rebalance call. Deletion is the substantive change: merge_subtrees (a
priority-ordered treap merge) becomes join_subtrees, which relinks the
in-order successor and rebalances back up. Double rotations are composed
from the two existing single rotations so the resummarize ordering that
keeps subtree summaries correct holds by construction.

PayoutNode.priority becomes PayoutNode.height, so the struct layout changes
and this is not upgrade-compatible — it must ship in the published package.
tick_priority is deleted, taking the bcs and blake2b256 imports with it.

Adds two test-only seams: root_height_for_testing and
assert_balanced_for_testing. The treap's priority was immutable and
re-derivable from the key, so it could not go stale; height is maintained
state, and a missed update degrades depth silently while every evaluator
still returns the correct number. That failure mode needs its own check.
Flagging the seams against unit-tests.md rule 18.

* predict: make the payout-tree suite pin the guarantee, not the happy path

A five-lens review of this branch found no correctness defect in the AVL
implementation, and one recurring gap: the tests exercised one of the four
rotation cases and asserted no payout value on the rewritten delete path.
Mutation testing put numbers on it — six plausible bugs shipped green,
including the inner-rotation tie-break, either double rotation, the
"write the demoted node first" ordering, and take_min dropping the
successor's right subtree. That last one reports a settled liability of
1500 against a true 2250, silently, with balance and node_count intact.

assert_balanced_for_testing only recomputed heights, so it could not fail
on an economic bug. It now recomputes search order, balance, every stored
height, every stored summary, and reachable node count, and returns the
height so the depth assertion comes from the same seam — replacing
root_height_for_testing rather than adding to it.

New coverage, each case chosen to kill a specific mutant rather than to
walk a path: descending and outside-in arrival reach the rotation cases
ascending fixtures never do; a delete-induced height tie pins the strict
'>' in both inner conditions, which no insert-only fixture can distinguish;
a successor carrying its own right subtree pins the one non-obvious pointer
move in join_subtrees, asserted on terms; and interleaved churn recomputes
the whole invariant after every operation. The GC test now asserts terms
against a rebuilt survivor tree, which is a real check here because the two
trees genuinely differ in shape.

Verified by re-running the mutants: all four previously-surviving ones now
fail. The old fixtures were also isomorphic to each other (both ascending,
same length), so the "adversarial vs honest" comparison could not fail for
any balancing scheme; that test is gone.

Also documents two invariants the review found load-bearing but unstated:
shape-independence holds for a consistent index, so the settlement walk's
underflow is not a desync detector; and combine_summaries' associativity
depends on max_net_payout_prefix_gain never exceeding net_start.

subject: predict: skip a market outside the flush's active set instead of aborting (DBU-679)
body:
The flush's market list is built off-chain before submitting, but
start_pool_valuation snapshots the active set at execution. Any settle-and-sweep in
between - rebalance_expiry_cash is permissionless, and the ordinary market roll
calls it - leaves the list holding a market the flush no longer covers, and
EExpiryMarketNotActive then failed the whole flush. Observed on testnet
predict-6-24 as repeated plp::assert_expiry_ready_to_value abort 0, about 13
failures in 3 hours; digest recorded in
evidence/rp27-flush-active-set-race-2026-07-30.md.

Both stages now return early for such a market. The completeness proof is
untouched: expected_expiry_markets is read ON-CHAIN, so it is authoritative and the
caller's list is only a hint about which commands to emit;
seal_valuation_snapshot requires a frozen pricer for every expected market and
finish_flush requires every expected market valued, so a market that genuinely
belongs to the flush still cannot be skipped. EExpiryMarketAlreadyValued is
unchanged and still guards double-counting, so assert_expiry_ready_to_value is
renamed to assert_expiry_not_already_valued for what it now does.
EExpiryMarketNotActive becomes unreachable and is removed.

The opposite direction - a market that ENTERS the active set after the list was
built - still aborts at the seal, and should: the flush would otherwise mark a pool
it had not fully valued. Market creation is lock-gated, so that window is small and
the retry is cheap.

Recorded as RP-27 with the duty inventory. The former abort test becomes the
regression test; mutation-checked - restoring the abort fails it.

subject: predict: give the flush's fee rates their own type, off the mark (DBU-688) (#1196)
body:
Review follow-ups from #1186. No behaviour change — 523/523 before and after.

C1. `new_flush_mark` took the NAV pair and both fee rates as four positional
`u64`s. That is the shape that previously let the supply rate reach both slots
while compiling, silently disabling the shipped withdrawal fee, and
`predict-contracts.md` asks coupled domain values to use a named object rather
than a run of same-typed primitives.

`FeeRates { supply, withdraw }` is now its own type and `FlushMark` is price-only
again, with the rates threaded alongside it into `drain`. What that buys:

- A rate can no longer be transposed into a NAV slot and still compile — the
  cross-class swap is now type-impossible rather than test-caught.
- `drain(mark, fees)` takes two distinct types instead of a four-value run.
- The 51 drain call sites name the leg they drive (`no_fees()`,
  `supply_fee(rate)`, `withdraw_fee(rate)`) instead of a positional pair.
- It makes #1186's claim — the fee is applied after the mark and never enters it
  — structural rather than documented.

What it does NOT buy, stated because an earlier draft of this message claimed
otherwise: swapping the two legs *within* the pair is no better detected than
before. The risk moved from `new_flush_mark` slots 3-4 to `new_fee_rates` slots
1-2, and `flush_freezes_both_configured_fee_rates` catches it in both cases —
verified by running the swap against the base, where it fails the same five
tests.

C4. `Fixture` captures the shared `ProtocolConfig` id at construction and the two
fee helpers retrieve it with `take_shared_by_id` (unit-tests Rule 13). Scoped to
the helpers this branch added: the fixture's other ambient `take_shared` calls are
pre-existing and left for a separate sweep rather than widened here.

Also corrects two doc lines this refactor invalidated — `fees-and-rebates.md` and
`configuration.md` both said the rates are frozen *into the mark*, which was true
when they were written and is not now.
rationale: only non-code files changed

subject: predict: charge an admin-configurable fee on PLP withdraw fills, entry free (DBU-688) (#1186)
body:
* predict: charge an admin-configurable fee on PLP supply and withdraw fills (DBU-688)

Adds `plp_fee_rate` to `ProtocolConfig`: one protocol-wide rate in
FLOAT_SCALING, default 1%, admin-settable inside a hard 0..5% envelope.

The fee is charged on the DUSDC leg of every executed LP fill and retained by
the pool, so it accrues to remaining PLP holders rather than the protocol
reserve. On supply it is deducted from the escrowed DUSDC before shares are
priced, so only the net buys PLP and the full escrow still joins idle. On
withdraw it is withheld from the marked payout, so the requester receives the
net while the full escrowed PLP is burned. Rounding is up, to the pool (R2).

Request-time `min_plp_out` / `min_dusdc_out` limits are compared against the
post-fee result, so a limit bounds what the requester actually receives.
Refunded, cancelled, and still-queued requests are never charged.

The rate is read once per flush into the frozen `FlushMark`, so every fill in
one flush is charged the same rate, and the setter is valuation-locked so it
cannot shift midway through a flush.

The fee never enters the mark: the mark stays the exact pool-wide NAV used in
both directions and the charge is applied after it. That is what separates it
from the superseded uncertainty-band withdraw fee of the approximate-NAV
design, which distorted the mark itself.

Events: `SupplyFilled` / `WithdrawFilled` gain `fee_dusdc`, and
`FlushExecuted` gains the `fee_rate` the flush froze. Both are additive.

Whether the fee should ship enabled, and at what rate, is not settled — see
predeploy open item P-27, which carries the experiment plan and decision rule.

* predict: default the PLP fee to 20 bps and pin the flush's config wiring (DBU-688)

Two changes on top of the fee itself.

Default `plp_fee_rate` is 20 bps (2_000_000), not 1%. The envelope is unchanged
at 0..5%, and the drain tests keep charging an explicit 1% because they pin the
fee arithmetic, not the shipped default; the default is asserted in the two
places that mean to assert it.

Adds `flush_freezes_the_configured_plp_fee_rate`, the missing coverage of the
wiring between the admin knob and the drain. The `lp_book` drain tests hand a
rate straight to `new_flush_mark`, so a `finish_flush` that ignored
`ProtocolConfig` and froze a constant passed all of them — verified: hard-coding
the flush to a zero rate left 475/475 green. The new flow test drives two real
flushes through the real admin path and asserts the rate each one froze, so it
catches both a missing read and a stale one. Restoring the hard-coded zero now
fails it.

Reading the frozen rate needs `vault_events::flush_executed_fee_rate`, a
`#[test_only]` event-fields reader following the existing propbook precedent —
the frozen rate is otherwise unobservable from Move.

* predict: restore Move.lock to a resolvable dependency graph

`packages/predict/Move.lock` on main carries a `[pinned.mainnet.*]` block that
pins `block_scholes_oracle`, a package no longer in the tree. `sui move build
--path packages/predict` therefore fails resolution before compiling anything:

    Error while loading dependency ../block_scholes_oracle:
    Invalid directory at `../block_scholes_oracle`

This is not specific to this branch — a pristine checkout of 44515604 fails the
same way. The block was added by 44515604 (#1184) and is local resolution state
a `sui move build` writes, not intentional pinning: 27f21909 has no such block
and builds. This restores that version, which is a pure deletion of the 66
generated lines.

Flagged rather than folded silently: the same fix belongs on main directly, and
this branch only carries it so the fee work can be built and tested at all.

* predict: pin the fee reported on supply and withdraw fill events

The balance assertions cannot see a wrong `fee_dusdc`. Shares and cash both come
from the quote's `output`, so an event reporting the wrong fee leaves every
balance assertion green while misattributing pool revenue to off-chain
consumers, which is where the charge is accounted from.

Found by mutation: reporting the whole request's fee on a partially-filled
supply, instead of the filled slice's, passed all 513 tests. It now fails
`supply_fill_reports_the_fee_charged_on_the_slice`.

Adds `#[test_only]` fee readers for both fill events, following the existing
propbook precedent for event-field readers, and asserts the reported figure on a
partial supply fill — where the slice fee and the whole request's fee differ —
and on a withdrawal.

* predict: fixes from the independent review of DBU-688

Two public docs still told users the pool charges no LP-side fee, which is now
false at HEAD and was the review's only High-severity class:
- `docs/risks.md` — the bullet also built a safety argument on the absence of a
  fee ("safe precisely because the mark is exact"). Rewritten: the mark is still
  exact and still dual-use, and the charge sits outside it.
- `docs/design/invariants.md` — asserted "no fee" as an invariant.

RP-23's "at most one ulp of idle is left behind" is no longer true with a fee
set; the register now carries the actual bound (the slice's fee plus the ulp) and
why the second inversion was declined. The matching source comment said the same
stale thing and is fixed with it.

`fee_on` relies on the envelope keeping the rate below 1.0 for `amount - fee`
never to underflow inside the mandatory flush, and that guarantee lived only in a
comment. `plp_fee_rate_envelope_cannot_reach_full_scale` pins it, so widening the
envelope fails a test instead of aborting a live flush.

Two coverage gaps on the highest-risk paths, both mutation-checked:
- the idle-short withdraw branch was only ever exercised at zero fee, so the
  gross inversion and its retained-fee bound were untested;
- no supply test carried both a limit and a fee, where the per-slice ceil'd fee
  meets the pro-rated limit at its exact boundary.

`plp_fee_rate` narrowed from `public` to `public(package)`: `ProtocolConfig` is a
shared object, so off-chain callers read the field directly, which is why the
equally SDK-relevant `max_lp_pool_value` is not public either. The `#[test_only]`
event readers move out of the `public(package)` block to the module end.

P-27 records the review's economics finding: because the fee is retained by the
pool, a supplier immediately refunds a share of it equal to their post-fill
ownership, so the effective rate is `F * (1 - share)` and tends to zero for the
largest LP — the actor best placed to time the mark pays the least of the charge
meant to price that timing. Calibration has to target the effective rate.

* predict: fixes from the second independent review of DBU-688

`liquidity-and-nav.md` still carried the pre-fee fill formulas. The earlier pass
edited that file's NAV-rework note but left the two formulas, both `min_*_out`
definitions, and the drain walkthrough describing a fee-free protocol — in the
file the other three docs point at for LP mechanics. An integrator sizing
`min_plp_out` from the documented formula would have been refunded every flush at
the shipped one-attempt setting.

P-27's worked example was arithmetically wrong: the holding is worth 9_989_989
and the net fee is 10_011, not 9_990_000 and 10_000. The identity it illustrates
(`F * (1 - post_fill_share)`) was right; only the numbers were not. Recorded the
closed form `F * V / (V + n - F)` alongside it so it can be rederived. (Note the
tempting `F * V / (V + n)` is NOT it — that drops the fee from the denominator
and understates the charge.)

"Accrues to the holders who stayed" was wrong on the supply leg: the payer is a
holder the instant the fill lands and immediately recaptures their post-fill
share, which is the whole point of the P-27 economics added in the same branch.
Corrected to pro-rata, with the withdraw leg still reading "stayed".

`plp_fee_rate_envelope_cannot_reach_full_scale` asserted two constants and called
nothing, which unit-tests Rule 5 names directly. Repl

subject: predict: correct RP-27's severity claim and cover the mixed stale-market case (DBU-679)
body:
Adversarial re-verification of the premise, by three independent agents. The
capacity concern and the fix both survived; the RP-27 severity claim did not.

RETRACTED: 'the flush has been failing continuously since 07-07'. The repo's own
contemporaneous records refute it - ledger 0003 items 39/50/60 record flushes
landing between the aborts that day, a clean failures10m=0.0 scan, and a
successful 9-market flush with an on-chain digest. At a ten-minute interval with
no fast retry, 13 failures in 3 hours means about 5 flushes still landed, and the
earlier occurrence ran nearer 1-in-8. The honest severity is an intermittent
liveness degradation of varying rate, not a standing outage; the ~6x rate change
with no flush-lane code change argues against one continuous phenomenon.

Two further corrections to the evidence record:
- abort 0 does not uniquely identify the sweep race. On the deployed build the
  set-membership check runs BEFORE the registration check, so an unregistered or
  wrong-vault market id lands on the same code. A double-value would raise code 1,
  so that is excluded, but the sweep attribution rests on the surrounding
  operational sequence, not on the code alone.
- the 'routine race' framing understated caller scheduling. A caller that defers

asset an underlying tracks — and that guard cannot be written while the spelling
is reachable only by fetching both store objects. Put it on the row now, bound
it to 32 bytes so a malformed input cannot be permanently baked into a value
re-hashed on every read, and say at the call site what no check can verify.

subject: predict/pricing: take log-moneyness as a difference of logs, deleting the digital-limit shortcuts (#1212)
body:
* predict/pricing: size the SVI envelope so the digital-limit saturations are exact

`compute_nd2` short-circuits on the strike/forward ratio alone: when
`strike * 1e9 / forward` truncates to zero it returns the exact digital limit
1e9, and when the product exceeds u64 it returns 0. Those limits are only true
while total variance is small. The envelope capped |a|, b, |m| and sigma at a
shared 100, which is a representability bound rather than a variance bound and
admits total variance above 36,000 — at which a deep-ITM strike's true digital
is 0.0 against a returned 1.0, a 100% absolute error on a number the mint's
entry probability, the liquidation threshold and the NAV mark all consume.

Size the caps per parameter against the error the contract can express:
|a|, sigma <= 1, b <= 0.1, |m| <= 10. The parameters do not enter variance
equally — `a` directly, `b` scaling the whole moneyness-dependent term, and
`m`/`sigma` only through `b` — so `m` holds the same budget at a looser bound.
Over the admissible box the worst deep-ITM saturation error is ~5.3e-11, i.e.
0.05 of one raw unit at the 1e9 scale the digital is returned in. The deep-OTM
saturation was already sound (~1.4e-11) and tightens only as a consequence.

Registered as RP-26, including why this does not re-open RP-15's rejection of a
tighter envelope: this bounds where Predict's own arithmetic shortcut claims to
be exact, not the surface's quality, and adds no g(k) >= 0 check.

Committed real surfaces sit 13x to 5,600x inside the new caps.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict/pricing: take log-moneyness as a difference of logs, deleting the digital-limit shortcuts

Reverts the SVI cap change in the previous commit and fixes the defect at its
source instead.

`compute_nd2` formed `strike * 1e9 / forward` and took `ln` of it. That quotient
destroys exactly the tails it is asked about: it floors to zero once strike is a
billionth of forward, leaves u64 once it is 1.8e10 times it, and just inside
those limits survives as a handful of raw units carrying tens of percent of
truncation error. The two short-circuits covering that returned the exact digital
limits 1e9 and 0 WITHOUT READING THE SURFACE — true only while total variance is
small, and silently wrong when it is not, on a value the mint's entry
probability, the liquidation threshold and the NAV mark all consume.

`ln` is defined across the whole positive u64 domain, so `ln(strike) -
ln(forward)` is well-conditioned over every representable pair: |k| <= 44.4
against the 20.7 the ratio form could reach, at 1e-7 relative error per term
rather than an error that grows without bound as the tail deepens. Both
short-circuits are deleted; the tails still reach their limits, now through d2's
existing normal-CDF clamp.

The previous commit's approach — capping the SVI envelope so the shortcut became
exact — is wrong twice over. Empirically, calibrated raw-SVI parameters for real
BTC surfaces reach b = 0.21 across maturities and b = 0.10, sigma = 1.00 within
the cadence ladder we trade, so those caps would have rejected real surfaces and
converted a latent correctness bug into a fail-closed pricing halt. Analytically,
Lee's moment formula makes b(1+|rho|) <= 2 a necessary no-arbitrage condition, and
a surface at that bound gives w = 41.4 and a true deep-ITM digital of exactly 0.5
against a returned 1.0 — so no envelope admitting arbitrage-free surfaces can make
the shortcut sound. max_svi_input stays at 100.

RP-26 rewritten accordingly. One differential assertion in the payout-tree walk
moves off a bit-equality that held only for the old path's price low bits, onto
the bound aggregation actually guarantees.

rationale: The commit removes a short‑circuit in compute_nd2 that returned extreme digital values (1e9 or 0) based solely on strike/forward ratio overflow/truncation, causing 100% pricing errors that fed into mint entry probability, liquidation thresholds and NAV marks. This mispricing could be exploited to trigger wrongful liquidations or mint at favorable prices, leading to financial loss, thus a security‑relevant bug fix.

subject: predict: ship DEEP staking benefits disabled by default (DBU-708) (#1214)
body:
* predict: ship DEEP staking benefits disabled by default (DBU-708)

Predict had no way to run without the staking programme. One benefit curve on
`ProtocolConfig.stake_config` scales with an account's active stake and drives
both the trading-fee discount (capped by the upgrade-required
`max_fee_discount`) and the settled trading-loss rebate share (uncapped on the
staking side). The `*_benefit_power` thresholds are admin-tunable, but their
validation envelope admits no setting that yields a zero benefit — the lowest
admissible `lower_benefit_power` still pays a proportional discount — so an
admin could not switch benefits off without a package upgrade.

Add an `enabled` master switch to `StakeConfig`, defaulting false, and gate
`benefit_ratio` on it. A freshly created protocol therefore charges every trader
the undiscounted fee and pays no stake-scaled rebate at any stake, including
above `upper_benefit_power`. `protocol_config::set_stake_benefits_enabled`
activates or deactivates the programme under `AdminCap`; the thresholds keep
their values across a toggle, so turning it on needs no re-tuning first.

The switch gates the shared ratio rather than either consumer, so both benefits
move together by construction — there is deliberately no setting that discounts
fees while withholding the rebate. Making `max_fee_discount` admin-tunable at
zero was rejected: it would leave the uncapped rebate live and would move an
upgrade-required constant into tunable config for no gain.

While benefits are off the rebate reserve still accrues at
`trading_loss_rebate_rate` and returns to the pool in full at settlement, since
no account is owed anything. Zeroing that rate is a separate operator action on
an already-tunable knob, not a code change.

Two flow tests asserted stake-driven amounts and now enable the programme in
their fixtures through the real admin path, so they still cover the discount and
the rebate rather than the new default.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict: format the stake-benefits test helper (DBU-708)

`set_stake_benefits_enabled` fits within the print width on one line, so the
multi-line signature it was written with fails `format:move:check`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict: freeze the stake-benefit switch per market at creation (DBU-708)

Review of the previous commit found that a live benefit switch is unsafe in the
disabling direction. Both staking benefits resolve after the trade that earns
them - the fee discount at mint, the loss rebate at a post-settlement claim - so
an admin disabling the programme while a settled backlog is unclaimed lets the
permissionless cleanout resolve every one of those accounts at zero. The claim
removes the account's expiry summary, so it is one-shot: re-enabling recovers
nothing, and the whole reserve has already gone to the pool.

Make that unrepresentable rather than an operator-ordering rule. StakeConfig now
holds `template_benefits_enabled`, each ExpiryMarket snapshots it at creation
into an immutable `stake_benefits_enabled`, and both benefit consumers read the
market's snapshot. A toggle therefore cannot reach a market already trading in
either direction: a market written under the programme honours it through
settlement and claim, and enabling phases in as new markets are created (about
one cadence period at 1m/5m/1h).

The benefit thresholds stay live, so retuning the curve still reaches markets
already trading. Only whether the programme applies is a contract term. The
admin entrypoint is renamed `set_template_stake_benefits_enabled` per the
template-naming rule for values that affect future objects only.

Also corrects two factual errors in the previous commit's documentation, both
found in review: the rebate reserve is released per account by the cleanout
after settlement, not in one release at settlement (the settled sweep holds it
back via `required_cash`); and `trading_loss_rebate_rate` is snapshotted per
expiry, so zeroing it binds only markets created after the change.

Pinned by settlement_flow_tests::
disabling_the_stake_benefit_template_cannot_zero_an_earned_rebate, verified to
fail when the claim is mutated to read the live template.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict: make the stake benefit a ratio that ships at zero (DBU-708)

Replaces the boolean benefit switch with a magnitude. `StakeConfig` gains
`max_benefit_ratio`, which scales the stake curve, so `benefit_ratio =
stake_curve(active_stake) * max_benefit_ratio`. It ships at 0, which is what
makes the programme inert on a fresh deployment: no fee discount, no
stake-scaled loss rebate, at any stake. "Off" is no longer a special mode, and
the programme can run at partial strength on the way up.

Also completes the freeze the previous commit started. Snapshotting only the
switch left the curve thresholds live, and the thresholds are read at claim
time - after the rebate was earned. Measured on the settlement flow: widening
the thresholds to their admissible maxima after the fees were paid cut a full
staker's earned rebate from 2_500_000 to 1_252_551, irreversibly, because the
claim removes the account's expiry summary. Each `ExpiryMarket` now snapshots
the whole `StakeConfig` at creation and prices both benefits against its own
copy, so neither the ratio nor the thresholds can reprice a contract already
written. This matches `StrikeExposureConfig`, already snapshotted per expiry for
the same reason, and moves `StakeConfig` from a live config to a contract-term
template in the docs.

Both admin entrypoints are `set_template_*`, per the naming rule for values that
affect future objects only. The snapshot also removed the last live-config read
from `claim_trading_loss_rebate` and `compute_mint_quote`, so their now-unused
`&ProtocolConfig` parameters are dropped.

Pinned by settlement_flow_tests::
retuning_the_stake_benefit_template_cannot_reprice_an_earned_rebate, which
retunes both the ratio and the thresholds after settlement and asserts the full
rebate is still paid. Verified to fail when the claim is mutated to read live
policy.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* predict: emit the stake snapshot and pin the mint-side freeze (DBU-708)

Two review findings, neither a defect in shipped behaviour.

MarketCreated now carries the market's stake policy — max_benefit_ratio and
both benefit powers — alongside the other creation-time snapshots it already
reports. The event exists so indexers can reconstruct per-market terms, and this
branch made stake policy per-market: without these fields a ratio-0 market is
indistinguishable from a full-strength one, so an indexer mis-computes trader
fees by up to the whole max_fee_discount and mis-computes rebate liability for
every account in the market. Event fields are frozen once deployed, so this is
addable only pre-deploy.

Adds the mint-side twin of the rebate regression test. The suite pinned the
rebate consumer end-to-end but nothing pinned the fee-discount consumer: every
fixture sets the template before create_expiry and never moves it before
minting, so re-threading &ProtocolConfig into compute_mint_quote left all 563
tests green while making mint pricing retro-repriceable again — the exact hazard
the snapshot exists to prevent. The new test creates the market while the
template pays nothing, raises the template, stakes to full benefit, rolls the
epoch so the stake is active, and asserts both the quote and the account debit
carry the undiscounted fee. Verified to fail, alone, when the mint path is
mutated to read live policy.
