subject: margin: migrate to Pyth's upgraded Core alongside legacy Pyth (DBU-668) (#1170)
body:
* margin: link Pyth Pro alongside legacy Pyth and read prices as values (DBU-668)

Pyth Core is being replaced by a separately published package on Sui, not an
in-place upgrade, so `pyth::price_info::PriceInfoObject` under Pyth Pro is a
different Move type. Repointing the import is therefore impossible: a
`compatible` upgrade cannot change a public function's parameter types, and
`compatible` is already the most permissive policy Sui offers.

Both packages are now linked at once. `rename-from` resolves the named-address
collision, so the legacy feed stays on `pyth::` and Pyth Pro is reachable as
`pyth_pro::`.

The oracle layer is restructured so the two feeds can share one pricing path.
Every guard - staleness, feed id, confidence interval, EWMA deviation - moves
into four readers that return a `PythReading` value:

  read_price / read_price_unsafe          (legacy feed)
  read_price_pro / read_price_pro_unsafe  (Pyth Pro)

Everything downstream of a reader is now pure arithmetic over that value, which
collapses each safe/unsafe pair into a single function: price_config,
calculate_usd_price, calculate_price, calculate_target_currency and
calculate_target_amount, plus margin_manager's risk_ratio_int and
assets_in_debt_unit. Four oracle functions and two margin_manager internals are
deleted outright; oracle.move loses 65 lines net.

No public signature changes and no behaviour change: the entrypoints still take
the legacy `&PriceInfoObject` and now read it at the top. The Pyth Pro readers
are unused until the `_pro` entrypoints land in the follow-up.

Feed ids are unchanged between Core and Pro (verified against Pyth's symbology
API for BTC, ETH, SUI, USDC, USDT and DEEP), so `CoinTypeData.price_feed_id`
needs no migration and the feed-id assert holds for both readers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* margin: add Pyth Pro entrypoints in _pro modules (DBU-668) (#1171)

* margin: add Pyth Pro entrypoints in _pro modules (DBU-668)

Adds the Pyth Pro half of the margin surface. Pyth Pro's `PriceInfoObject` is a
different Move type from the legacy feed's, so the existing entrypoints can
never accept it - their signatures are frozen by the `compatible` upgrade
policy. The Pro surface therefore lives in two new modules under the same
function names:

  deepbook_margin::margin_manager_pro   12 entrypoints
  deepbook_margin::pool_proxy_pro        8 entrypoints

Callers switch module, not function name.

Each existing entrypoint keeps its exact signature and now delegates to a
`public(package)` `_core` that takes `PythReading` values instead of feed
objects. The Pro entrypoint reads the Pro feed and calls the same core, so both
feeds run byte-identical logic - there is no second copy of the borrow,
withdraw, liquidation or order-placement paths to keep in sync.

The internals that previously threaded feed objects now thread readings:
tpsl::add_conditional_order, process_collected_orders_v2/v3, and pool_proxy's
solvency and monotonicity helpers. That is what allows one core to serve both
feeds.

Nothing is removed. Both feeds go through `get_price_no_older_than`, so the
legacy entrypoints fail closed on their own once the legacy feeds stop
updating; no teardown is needed at the cutover.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* margin: restore lazy oracle reads and close review findings (DBU-668)

An independent review found the entrypoint-level reads introduced by the seam
refactor were stricter than origin/main on paths that must stay available.
Fixes, each restoring the pre-Pyth-Pro behaviour exactly:

Confidence bound is a pricing guard again, not a read guard. It moves back out
of the reader and into `price_config`, where main had it, carried on
`PythReading.conf: Option<u64>`. A telemetry read (the deposit event) therefore
cannot be rejected for a wide interval, and unvalidated reads skip it as they
always did.

`withdraw` no longer reads unconditionally. It takes two independently optional
reading pairs: validated ones, only when the manager carries debt; unvalidated
ones, only when a base/quote asset is withdrawn. A debt-free withdrawal now
touches no oracle at all, so a stale feed can no longer stop a user reclaiming
collateral.

`deposit` reads only the deposited asset's own feed, and nothing for a DEEP
deposit, matching main. It no longer requires the other side of the pair to be
fresh.

`risk_ratio` / `risk_ratio_unsafe` short-circuit to MAX for a manager with no
borrow position, without consulting the oracle - restoring the read-only view
for indexer and devInspect callers during a feed outage.

Also from the review:
- Move.lock testnet section re-pinned; it previously carried no
  PythProCompatible/WormholeSimpleMajority entries, so the dependency set the
  testnet deploy would actually use was not in the diff. margin_liquidation's
  lock updated likewise. Incidental Sui framework drift reverted - a bump past
  CI's SUI_VERSION has broken this suite before.
- risk_ratio_unsafe_core deleted; it was byte-identical to risk_ratio_core.
  Safety is the reader's job, so one core serves both.
- Five Pyth Pro reader tests added, with a build_pyth_pro_price_info_object
  helper, covering happy path, staleness, feed-id mismatch, the confidence
  bound, and that an unvalidated reading skips it.
- Stale comment fixed at pool_proxy.move:165.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* margin: close audit findings - lazy pool_proxy reads, deposit reader, lockfiles (DBU-668)

A second independent audit found the eager-read regression again, in the
entrypoints the first pass did not cover, plus an over-correction in the
deposit fix.

pool_proxy: place_limit_order_v2, place_market_order_v2 and
place_market_order_and_repay_loan read the oracle unconditionally, but every
consumer is debt-gated - assert_post_trade_solvent early-returns without debt,
and the monotonic gate no-ops. So a debt-free manager, which on main placed
orders with zero oracle reads, could be blocked by a stale feed on the busiest
entrypoints. The three cores and the two helpers now take Option<PythReading>
and unwrap after their own debt gate, so the gate and the unwrap live in the
same function and cannot disagree. The four reduce-only entries are unchanged:
their direction guard already requires debt, so they always read on main too.

deposit: the previous fix over-corrected to the unvalidated reader, dropping
staleness and EWMA from a read main validated. main used get_pyth_price
(staleness + feed id + EWMA, confidence deliberately skipped), so the validated
reader is restored - the narrowing to the deposited asset's own feed and the
confidence bound living in price_config both stand, which is what main did.

Move.lock: margin_liquidation's mainnet section regenerated (it had no
PythProCompatible/WormholeSimpleMajority pins and a stale root digest, so a
mainnet build re-resolved a moving tag instead of a pin). The unrelated mainnet
Wormhole rev flip is reverted - verified not required, mainnet still builds.
Framework drift reverted again on both locks.

Also fixes the invalid-documentation-comment warning introduced on
deposit_core's parameter.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* margin: behavioural tests for the Pyth Pro entrypoints (DBU-668)

The _pro surface had build-only coverage: a swapped base/quote argument or a
downgraded reader compiled and passed CI. These drive the same flows as the
legacy tests through the Pro feed.

Covers deposit, borrow_base, borrow_quote, withdraw, risk_ratio,
risk_ratio_unsafe, manager_state, manager_states, update_current_pri
rationale: The commit only migrates to a new Pyth package, restructures oracle readers, and adds entrypoints without changing any public signatures or behavior. It is a refactor/feature addition, not a correction of incorrect behavior, and the diff shows no security-relevant logic changes.

subject: predict: carry the difference-of-logs change into the parity model and the docs (#1220)
body:
Follow-up to #1212, from two independent reviews of the merged change. The
contract math was found correct with large headroom on every type boundary; these
are the consequences outside pricing.move that the original change missed.

The blocking one: simulations/python_replay.py still implemented the deleted code
path. It is the bit-exact off-chain model that harness/parity.py and sim.ts drive
and compare_parity.py compares field-by-field, and its comment claimed to "mirror
pricing.move exactly" while computing `ln(strike * 1e9 / forward)` with both
digital-limit short-circuits. The divergence was not confined to the tails — k
differed at every off-forward strike, propagating through mul_down(price,
quantity) into shares_minted — so the next parity run would have failed broadly
and blamed the chain. Now takes the difference of logs; verified it reproduces the
contract at both tails (0 on the high-variance surface where it previously
returned 1e9, 1e9 on an ordinary one).

Also corrected, all documentation of behaviour that no longer exists:

- docs/concepts/pricing-and-oracles.md and docs/design/decisions.md described the
  ratio saturation as current design.
- RP-26 claimed the new form is "strictly better everywhere". The error BOUND is
  uniformly better, but pointwise the difference form is less accurate on ~13% of
  sampled pairs by up to 1.2e-8. Restated to the defensible claim, with the
  measurement. Both it and the pricing.move comment also gave the ratio form's
  reach as 20.7, which is only its negative reach; positively it reached +23.64.
- Two pricing_guard_tests docstrings still named the deleted control flow as the
  reason for their assertions.
- The payout-tree walk bound is `<= GC_SURVIVOR_COUNT`, not one less: with no
  shared boundary each order floors independently. It equals 1 today only because
  survivor A's quantity is exactly 1e9, making mul_down the identity — a
  coincidence of the same class as the bit-equality it replaced.

Two items are owed rather than fixed, filed as P-28 and P-29: the committed
reference tolerances were derived under the old error model (regeneration needs
the gitignored scenario dataset), and the C-1 capacity model has not been
re-measured for the added ln.

rationale: only non-code files changed

subject: predict: correct the persistence claims and disclose the routine trading pause (DBU-679)
body:
Independent verification refuted the 'no permissionless path' framing in RP-27,
RP-28 and constants.move. A bare retry does change nothing and there is no
partial-flush escape, but relief does not require a successful flush:
rebalance_expiry_cash is permissionless and sweeps a settled market out of the
active set on its own, and remove_range frees a node whenever a strike tick empties
through a close or a liquidation. The claim that survives is narrower and worth
stating precisely - no path shrinks a LIVE market's tree on demand, because a 1x
position is closable only by its owner and is never liquidatable, so a poisoned
live market holds until it expires.

risks.md disclosed the trading pause only inside the bullet about ABANDONED
flushes, which understated it: the pause is a routine per-cycle cost, not a failure
mode. Now stated on its own terms, including that its wall-clock share scales with
flush cadence - a fast cadence trades LP-fill latency against trading availability,
a choice that did not exist when the flush was one transaction.

Verified: build --warnings-are-errors clean, predict 585/585, check.py clean,
format-move clean.

rationale: only non-code files changed

subject: predict: fix the off-chain surfaces the leverage removal broke (DBU-719) (#1239)
body:
* predict: fix the off-chain surfaces the leverage removal broke (DBU-719)

Stacked on #1237. The Move packages are self-consistent across #1236 and #1237,
but nothing type-checks a move-call target string or a name-keyed event field, so
three off-chain breaks reached HEAD invisibly.

Blocking, silent: harness/ts/strategy.ts matched `expiry_market:1` to detect
EFullCloseRequired and retry with a full close. #1237 deletes that code and
renumbers EMarketNotSettled into slot 1, so the harness would have read 'market
not settled' as 'retry with a full close' and resubmitted a live redeem against a
settled market. The retry is removed rather than repointed: after #1237 a live
redeem on a settled market aborts while loading the pricer, which the existing
non-terminal path already defers.

Blocking, loud: devtools/ts/runtime.ts still passed close_quantity to
redeem_settled_permissionless (deleted in #1237) and leverage to
mint_exact_quantity (deleted in #1236) — every cleanout and every harness mint
failed on argument count.

Silent metric corruption: strategy.ts read ev.parsedJson.net_premium; the
OrderMinted field is now premium, and event JSON is name-keyed, so it was writing
NaN into campaign records.

Also removes machinery whose subject no longer exists: the keeper's liquidate lane
and trade-liquidation-budget ladder, the liqChurn and liqBudget strategies, the
'liquidated' cleanup profile, the resolver's admission-leverage cap and its
leverage term in quantity sizing, and the leverage field threaded through
Instruction/MintLeg/Held.

Docs and registers now match HEAD: the binding rule in predict-contracts.md named
three renamed identifiers; RP-19 and RP-14 are live entries naming renamed and
deleted ones; markets-and-positions claimed SettledOrderRedeemed still carries the
settlement price. Two were my own misses from #1236 rather than #1237's doing —
liquidity-and-nav still documented the leveraged floor correction in full, and a
live NAV decision in decisions.md still described the correction scan.

Not done here, deliberately: simulations/python_replay.py is the independent parity
oracle the contracts are checked against, and it should not be migrated by an
author of the contract change. Until it is, trigger-benchmark stays red and no
post-removal gas figure can be measured.

Verified: 12 packages / 1,653 Move tests, tsc unchanged at 20 pre-existing
dependency errors (zero new, compared against the branch point), harness and
predeploy Python suites, predeploy/check.py, predict-audit preflight. Move
formatting reverted outside packages/predict — 17 files in deepbook/margin/propbook
carry pre-existing drift that belongs in its own PR (move.md, deepbookv3#1126).

* predict: pin that a settled order cannot be redeemed twice

With the settled close-terms token removed in #1237, predict_account's
remove_position is the sole mechanism stopping a second settled redeem from
releasing the same payout liability again — and nothing pinned it.

The replay needs its own transaction: the helper returns the shared
AccountRegistry, which is not takeable again until the next tx.

* predict: repair the harness trace schema, cash-backing coverage, and stale references (DBU-719)

`harness/ts/strategy.ts` emits the mint trace field `premium`, but `analyze.py`'s
schema still required `leverage` and `netPremium` and rejects unknown fields.
Every mint record therefore failed validation, so every campaign died at

that minted. Nothing connected the emitting TypeScript to the validating Python,
so `tsc`, the Move suites and CI all stayed green. `test_trace_schema.py` now
parses the trace literals out of the emitters and checks them against the schema
that will judge them; it fails against the pre-fix schema, naming `premium`.

`expiry_market::assert_cash_backing` has six call sites and no test could reach
any of them — `EInsufficientCash` had only leaf-unit coverage on a standalone
`ExpiryCash`. Two flow tests pin the mint and close sides. The close case:
closing a disjoint book's DOWN side pays out its live value (~0.5e9 at the
money) while the reserve only falls from 1.25e9 to the surviving order's own
1e9, so a market holding the legal minimum must refuse it.

References to code that no longer exists, each verified against source:
`strike_payout_tree::payout_terms` and `payout_terms_from_order` (six sites,
including two rule files and the audit skill's ownership carve-out) do not exist

RP-13 declared its accepted inaccuracy gone while its pinning-test and
reopen-when bullets still described it, and `config_constants` carried the same
dead rationale. RP-10 and RP-11 carry MEASURED figures taken over leveraged
mints; both now say so, and RP-11's liquidated arm is marked unrepeatable.
Four blast-radius lists still named liquidation as a live consumer.

The harness README documented four deleted strategies as working commands.
Removed the dead `NO_LEVERAGE_WINDOW_MS`, `ADMISSION_K`, `liquidationLtv` and
`ltvCap`, the always-zero `nLiquidated` cleanout split, and unused imports in

subject: predict: remove the DEEP stake fee discount (DBU-728) (#1243)
body:
* predict: remove the DEEP stake fee discount (DBU-728)

DEEP stake bought two things: a discount on the trading fee and a share of the
settled trading-loss rebate, both riding one benefit_ratio curve that ships at
max_benefit_ratio = 0. This removes the fee half and keeps the rebate.

- stake_config: fee_amount_after_discount deleted; constants::max_fee_discount
  deleted with it. benefit_ratio now feeds rebate_amount alone.
- expiry_market: compute_mint_quote drops its active_stake parameter and prices
  the fee StrikeExposureConfig computes; mint_prepared drops it too, so neither
  mint entrypoint rolls the account's stake epoch. Live redeem no longer rolls
  or discounts; the raw fee is still clamped at the redeem amount, now for the
  plain reason that a close must not cost more than it releases.
- tests: the two quote_mint tests whose subject was the discount are dropped
  (the market-snapshot freeze stays pinned on the rebate side by
  settlement_flow_tests::retuning_the_stake_benefit_template_cannot_reprice_an_
  earned_rebate); stake_config_tests exercises the same curve and bounds through
  rebate_amount.
- docs/registers: fees-and-rebates section 5 becomes the benefit curve feeding
  the rebate; decisions.md records the removal and marks the superseded
  entries; RP-11's late-stake reasoning and reopen condition are updated —
  with the fee side gone the rebate is the whole of staking's value rather than
  half of it, so the epoch activation gate is the only remaining bound on the
  late-stake leak.

subject: predict: add a tick-weighted first moment to the payout tree (DBU-732)
body:
The payout tree's subtree summaries carry no positional information: every
field is a function of the ordered (local_start, local_end) pairs, so two
orders of equal quantity spanning one tick and eighty ticks produce identical
summaries. That makes the area under the payout profile unreadable, and area
is what any spread statistic over the profile needs.

Carry sum(tick * local_start) and sum(tick * local_end) per subtree and expose
range_payout_sum, which reads the area over a tick range in O(log n) from the
same two traversals range_max_payout already performs.

The new terms are plain sums, so associativity — and with it the tree's
shape-independence — holds unconditionally rather than by a bound on magnitude,
which is also why they are u128: one term reaches pos_inf_tick times the max
order quantity, past u64.

subject: predict: add the quote calibration table, its validation and resolution (DBU-733)
body:
Adds `quote_calibration`, the module owning the correction tables a permissioned
keeper publishes and the policy bounding what one may do. Nothing reads it yet:
no entrypoint, no capability, and no pricing path is wired, so this changes no
behaviour.

A table maps a quoted probability to a corrected one, sampled on nine times to
expiry by nineteen probability knots and stored row-major. The time grid is a
constant because its coordinates are what a keeper fits to; the probability grid
is regular, so knots are indexed by division rather than stored, and the
endpoints m(0) = 0 and m(1) = 1 are implicit.

Publishing validates two things, and they are the whole safety argument: every
knot sits within `max_deviation` of the probability it corrects, and every row is
non-decreasing. Both survive resolution and application, because each later step
is a weighted average of validated values. A corrected probability is therefore
within `max_deviation` of its input at every probability and every remaining
time, not only at grid points, and a corrected surface is never less monotone
than the surface it came from.

Resolution across time is one rule: interpolate linearly in inverse time to
expiry against a virtual identity row at infinite time. Inside the grid that is
`k_lo * (k_hi - t) / (t * (k_hi - k_lo))` on the lower row, written without
forming a reciprocal; beyond the longest key the same expression collapses to
`k_max / t`, so a distant market's correction decays smoothly toward none rather
than clamping, and no second constant is needed.

Quotes fall back to the uncorrected price when the switch is off, an underlying
has no table, or a table has aged out — all protocol-wide states. Pricing against
a table the current transaction published aborts instead, because falling back
there would let the publisher alone quote outside the correction while
publishing only tables every bound accepts.

subject: predict: overwrite a published calibration row in place (DBU-733)
body:
Publishing removed the underlying's row and added a fresh one, which is two
dynamic-field operations — delete the old field object, create a new one — and
gives the row a new object identity on every publish. It was written that way
only because a table value without `drop` cannot be assigned over.

The ability set was the thing to fix. A published row is policy data with no
custody attached, so nothing needs the compiler forcing explicit disposal of it;
with `drop` the row is overwritten in place and a publish costs one field
mutation. Constructing the whole struct rather than assigning its fields
individually keeps the completeness check, so a later field cannot be silently
left stale.

subject: predict: add the capability and entrypoint that publish a calibration correction (DBU-733)
body:
Makes the calibration tables reachable for the first time. Pricing still does not
read them, so this changes no quote.

`QuoteCalibrationCap` carries authority to publish corrections and nothing else,
allowlisted on `Registry` beside the pause and lifecycle capabilities. Minting is
version-gated because it grants authority; revocation is not, so a keeper can be
cut off even from a package version below the runtime floor — the same asymmetry
the other two capabilities already use.

`registry::publish_quote_calibration` is the entrypoint, shaped like the existing
capability-gated entries: it owns the flow gates, and `ProtocolConfig` owns the
state transition and the events, while `quote_calibration` keeps ownership of
what a publishable table is. It is refused during a full-pool valuation, like
every other value a flush reads mid-transaction, but deliberately not gated on
trading pause: a correction creates no risk, and an operator may want it current
before trading resumes.

Two events. A publication carries the whole table, so an indexer can rebuild the
correction in force at any moment without reading protocol state. Policy changes
carry all three settings whichever one moved, so that stream alone is the current
policy; the three setters share one emitter rather than each assembling it.

subject: predict: apply the published calibration correction to every quote (DBU-733)
body:
Wires the corrections into pricing. A snapshot resolves the underlying's
correction once, to that market's remaining time, and carries it; every strike
priced in the transaction is then corrected alike.

The correction is applied where the digital at a single strike is formed, which
is the one point both public reads funnel through. That placement is what keeps
the flows consistent: `range_price` differences two corrected boundaries rather
than correcting a raw difference, so mint admission, live close, per-order value,
and the NAV walk all read the same corrected atom, and no flow reads a corrected
price while another reads a raw one. Settlement takes no snapshot at all and is
structurally out of reach.

`load_live_pricer` resolves the correction immediately after validating the
market's oracle bindings, since that is where the market's binding to its
underlying is already established. Its `PricingConfig` parameter is renamed
`pricing_config`: with a second configuration beside it, `config` read as though
it were the container of both.

`expiry_market::load_live_pricer` keeps its signature, so no transaction or SDK
shape changes, and it now documents the publish-provenance abort beside the
oracle one it already described — both refuse the atomic write-then-price and
neither prohibits reading state an earlier transaction wrote.

Two tidies found while checking the surface: the pricing module doc now mentions
the correction, and the knot-count helper drops to private, which is all its only
caller needs. One test helper takes the new argument so the suite still compiles;
no test coverage is added here.

Applying the correction consistently prevents inconsistent price reads that an attacker could manipulate, qualifying it as a security fix.

subject: predict: bound the correction when it is applied, not when it is published (DBU-733)
body:
Publication rejected any knot sitting further than `max_deviation` from the
probability it corrects. That put a hard abort between a keeper and an honest
measurement: the largest miscalibration this work exists to correct is 0.098 at
oracle price 0.30 (`predeploy/evidence/o1-oracle-calibration.md`), which lands
exactly on a grid knot, two thousandths under the default cap. A slightly finer
fit, or ordinary resampling noise, and the keeper simply fails to publish.

The bound now applies where it means something. Publication validates shape and
order only; a correction is clamped to `max_deviation` as it is applied, so an
oversized fit is truncated rather than refused. Clamping a non-decreasing
correction between two bounds that both rise with the input leaves it
non-decreasing, so the surface keeps the monotonicity the payout walk relies on,
and the bound is now true by inspection at the point of use rather than by an
argument about weighted averages.

Two things follow. The cap is read from configuration when a row is resolved, so
lowering it takes effect on the next quote instead of leaving already-published
corrections governed by whatever bound held when they landed. And the deviation
abort is gone, leaving four error codes where there were five.

The time grid now reaches fifteen minutes, adding ten- and fifteen-minute keys.
That is the horizon the calibration evidence actually covers; the grid stopped at
five, so across two thirds of the measured window most of a fitted correction was
being decayed away before it was applied.

Also reframes the ratified pricing and valuation deviation ceilings, which are
about evaluation error — how far the on-chain arithmetic lands from the true
real-math value of the function the pricing path is specified to compute. They
say nothing about whether that function is the right one, which is a question
answered against realized outcomes rather than against a reference implementation
of the formula itself. The ceilings keep their force over the corrected path: the
fixed-point result must still sit within 0.1% of the true evaluation of formula
plus correction, and the independent reference owes that coverage.

The fix clamps the correction instead, preventing the abort and thus mitigating a potential availability issue.

subject: predict: publish a correction only for a registered underlying (DBU-733)
body:
Publishing accepted any u32. A mistyped identifier stored a correction under a
key nothing reads, emitted an ordinary publication event, and left the intended
underlying quoting uncorrected — a silent failure with a plausible-looking
success on chain.

The entrypoint now requires the underlying to be one admin has approved for
Predict markets, checked alongside the other object-binding validation and before
any state changes. `MarketManager` owns that fact and kept it private, so it
exposes a package-level assertion rather than having the registry reconstruct it;
the entrypoint already held the registry, so nothing new is threaded through. As
a side effect the stored corrections are now bounded by the number of approved
underlyings instead of by the keeper's imagination.

Also drops the guard against a publication timestamped ahead of the clock. The
clock is non-decreasing and an earlier transaction wrote the value, so the
staleness subtraction below is already the invariant check — and if clock
semantics ever changed, aborting there is a better failure than silently dropping
the correction, which is what the guard did.

No per-underlying removal path: an operator turns the correction off protocol-wide
with the existing switch, a keeper retires one underlying's correction by
publishing the identity, and anything unattended ages out on the staleness window.

subject: predict: follow the existing config-event line, and collapse the pricing wrappers (DBU-733)
body:
Three cleanups from review, none of them behavioural.

The calibration setters emitted a policy event carrying all three settings. That

`up_price` and `range_price` had become wrappers that only reroute. Before the

`Pricer.calibration` is renamed `quote_correction`. Five lines below it the same

subject: predict: record the calibration trust, and open a seam for testing the bound (DBU-733)
body:
`risks.md` had no row for the capability that publishes corrections, and its
trust table exists precisely so a reader can enumerate who moves a price. It now
carries one, plus a section stating the position plainly: this is a correction to
how prices are formed rather than a product knob layered above them, it is prior
to everything downstream of a price including pool NAV, and that trust is
accepted deliberately and bounded rather than eliminated.

The flush-starter row needed amending for the same reason. It promised the mark
"cannot be set to anything but the pool's exact NAV at that instant", which was
true when pricing had one authority; NAV is downstream of quoted probabilities,
so a second actor now contributes to what that instant's NAV is. The row and the
section below it say so.

The plan document described the design before the bound moved: nine time keys, a
publish-time deviation check, and a bound resting on an argument about weighted
averages. It now describes eleven keys, validation covering shape and order only,
and a bound true by inspection at the point of use — for every table publication
admits, including one whose knots sit nowhere near the probabilities they
correct.

Adds a test-only constructor for a resolved row. The clamp is the whole safety
bound and it lives in `apply`, which was otherwise unreachable from a test
without publishing a table and advancing a transaction to escape the
publish-provenance guard. Also states the `float_scaling == (knot_count + 1) *
knot_step` identity that the interval index and both pinned endpoints rest on;
changing either constant alone indexes past the end of a row on the per-quote
path.

subject: predict: correct the documentation the calibration change falsified (DBU-733)
body:
Four documents described behaviour the code does not have.

`docs/concepts/pricing-and-oracles.md` owns the price formula and stated it with
no correction stage, and called the mint bounds a raw-probability envelope when
the value checked is the corrected one. Both now say what the code does, and the
correction is named as its own step so a reader sees where in the derivation it
sits.

`docs/risks.md` bounded the keeper at `max_deviation` on "any probability". That
holds for a single probability but not for a range, which is the thing holders
mint and the pool marks: a range is a difference of two separately corrected
probabilities, so a correction pushing one boundary up and the other down moves
it by twice the bound. That is the mechanism working rather than a gap in it —
the miscalibration being corrected is itself two-sided, so a range straddling the
crossover is wrong at both ends — but twice the bound is the number to size risk
against, and the page an evaluator reads did not carry it. The sharper corner is
now stated too: a correction flat across a band prices a range at exactly zero,
which refuses new mints there, quotes an existing holder's exit at nothing, and
marks those positions at zero in pool value.

The same page listed capability revocation among the things that bound the
keeper. Revocation stops the next publication, not the standing one, which keeps
applying until it ages out. Recovery is protocol-wide by design: there is
deliberately no per-underlying discard, so the switch is the only fast remedy and
the page now says so rather than implying a narrower tool exists.

`docs/design/configuration.md` owns the config taxonomy and the governance table
and had no mention of any of this — three admin-tunable values and a capability
holder had landed without it.

The plan document had drifted from its own implementation: it gave the far-decay
law as `300s / tte` when the grid now reaches 900, which would have had a keeper
fitting a correction three times too weak; it promised all three setters emit
events, which this PR's own event decision made false; and it named two functions
that no longer exist. Its insertion-point rationale was also wrong on the
mechanics, arguing from the infinity sentinels when the real reason is that
`up_price` is the one point both public reads funnel through.

Drops `row_for_testing`. It built rows publication cannot produce — one of them
underflow-aborts in `apply` — so a test written through it could report a defect
no keeper can trigger, while the composition that needs covering went untested.
Tests will drive publication and a later transaction instead, which is what the
code actually does.

subject: predict: cover the quote calibration correction (DBU-733)
body:
Twenty-six tests over what the correction does, none of which existed: every
prior test in the package runs with the mechanism switched off, so the whole
corrected path was unexercised.

Every test drives publication and then resolution in a later transaction, which
is the only composition production performs — pricing refuses a correction its
own transaction wrote. That is also why there is no test-only constructor: one
would manufacture rows publication cannot produce, and a test through it could
report a defect no keeper can trigger.

Covers all eight new abort codes, the three states that yield an uncorrected
price, the staleness boundary on both sides, resolution below the shortest key,
between keys, at the longest, and decaying past it, and the two structural
properties — that a correction moves a probability by at most the configured
bound and never makes the map decrease — exercised over the shapes validation
actually admits rather than one well-behaved example. Expected values are hand
derived from the interpolation rule with the arithmetic shown.

Two behaviours are pinned because they are surprising rather than because they
are complex: publication accepts a correction larger than the cap, since size is
policy applied when a quote is priced; and a correction flat across a band
prices a range at exactly zero, which is the sharp corner of applying a bound
per probability to a quantity built from two of them.

The suite was mutation-tested rather than trusted for passing: dropping the
clamp, loosening the staleness comparison, decaying against the wrong key, and
removing the row-order check each turn exactly the tests that should catch them
red.

subject: predict: strengthen the first-moment tests and guard an inverted range (DBU-732)
body:
The width test added with the query did not pin it: an order at tick 1 stores a
term of ~4e13, and the returned sum is built in u128 regardless of what the
fields hold, so u64 fields passed. Move the order to the top of the ladder, where
the stored term reaches ~4.6e22 and u64 aborts in boundary_summary. Verified by
flipping both fields to u64 and confirming the suite goes red.

The insertion-order test compared a tree against itself: both sequences produce
the identical shape, root 7 with identical children. Replace it with a
construction-path test over the same final book, and put the real shape evidence
where genuinely different shapes already exist — boundary_gc_preserves_terms_and_balance
compares a 66-node rotation-churned tree against a rebuilt one.

Extend the sweep to an open-upper leg over a nonzero open-lower prefix and to
adjacent orders sharing a boundary tick, the two surfaces it did not reach.

An inverted range now aborts instead of silently returning zero. An empty window
is a legitimate zero; reversed arguments are a caller bug, and for a charge built
on this read the silent path would price a trade at nothing.

Correct three comments: the field doc had the area subtraction backwards and only
valid when start and end totals match, the query doc called a discrete integral a
second moment, and a test comment described rebalances the fixture does not
perform. Soften the underflow claim — it tests the aggregate, not each prefix, so

subject: predict: cover draining, stacked boundaries, and a deep tree (DBU-732)
body:
Three cases the existing fixtures could not reach. Draining every order must
return the area to zero rather than a residue left by reclaimed nodes, and the
tree must stay usable afterwards. Several orders sharing one lower boundary
aggregate into a single node, so the tick is weighted once against the summed
quantity rather than once per order. A tree built from interleaved ascending and
descending inserts rotates repeatedly, where the small fixtures stay near-flat.

The deep tree checks a spread of windows rather than every pair: a full sweep
over its domain is ~10^5 evaluations and exceeds the test gas budget.

subject: predict: measure inventory skew over a reference-centred window (DBU-732)
body:
Skew is the standard deviation of the payout profile across a window centred on
the market's reference tick. Occupancy prices how much reserve a position ties
up and is blind to where on the ladder it sits, so a trade that flattens the
book is charged nearly the same as one that concentrates it.

The window half-width is a fraction of the reference tick. Because a tick is a
price over tick_size, a fraction of the tick is the same fraction of price, so
one configured value covers every underlying and price level rather than needing
a tick count maintained per market.

Two accumulators carry sum(W) and sum(W^2) over the window, folded on every mint
and close so the statistic never walks the tick ladder. The variance uses the
single-division form, which is non-negative by Cauchy-Schwarz where dividing
first and squaring after can floor below zero and need a clamp.

The adjustment carries its own sign: a mint that flattens the book and a close
that unbalances it both invert the usual direction, so the flow cannot imply it.

Ships inert at a zero rate, which short-circuits before any tree read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The change introduces new configuration parameters and related getters/setters for inventory skew measurement; it adds functionality rather than correcting existing incorrect behavior, so it is not a bug fix and does not address a security issue.

subject: predict: scale the skew window with the square root of the tenor (DBU-732)
body:
A single window fraction across cadences measures the wrong thing at short
tenors. A one-minute market settles within a fraction of a percent, so a window
sized for a daily market spans hundreds of standard deviations and dilutes the
statistic toward zero: skew falls as one over the square root of the window, so
a window a hundred times too wide compresses the charge roughly tenfold. Short
tenors carry more pickoff risk, not less, so under-charging them is backwards.

Scale the configured fraction by the square root of the cadence period over one
day. Because the plausible move scales the same way, the window spans the same
number of standard deviations at every cadence, and a new cadence needs no new
configuration. At a 10% daily anchor and BTC's recent realized volatility of
roughly 2% daily, that is about five standard deviations everywhere.

The rule assumes independent, identically distributed returns. Crypto returns
are fat-tailed and cluster, which makes the true short-horizon deviation larger
than the rule implies, so the derived window runs slightly narrow at short
tenors. The anchor is sized with headroom rather than at the target.

A market whose plausible range spans too few ticks has no window to average over
and reads zero. Skew is undefined on a handful of settlement outcomes, and no
charge is the safe response.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: [MEV] The change fixes a mis‑scaled skew window that caused under‑charging for short‑tenor positions, which could be exploited by attackers to obtain cheap fees and drain protocol funds. Adding cadence_period_ms and scaling the window fraction mitigates this economic attack.

subject: predict: charge and rebate inventory skew (DBU-732)
body:
Wire the statistic into the trade paths. Mint and live close both carry a signed
adjustment: a mint that flattens the book is rebated and a close that unbalances
it is charged, so the direction is data rather than lifecycle. Both events carry
a charge and a rebate field, at most one of which is nonzero.

Charges sit in their own escrow alongside the inventory-impact reserve. Required
cash covers both and free cash nets out both, so neither is spendable or visible
in NAV while the market is live, and settlement releases the residual into
ordinary surplus. Cumulative collections equal the current statistic by
construction, so a rebate can never exceed what the same book already paid in.

A mint has no outbound payment leg, so a rebate reduces the withdrawal rather
than paying the trader, rejoining the payment before any split reads it. A
rebate larger than everything else the mint owes aborts instead of clamping: a
clamp would move the statistic without crediting the trader the difference,
which is what made the earlier finite-reserve design path-dependent. The abort is
unreachable at sane rates, since the trading fee floor alone exceeds any
plausible rebate.

Tests pin the exact deviation by hand rather than by direction: one order over

the deviation is Q/2 and a 20% rate charges 1e8. Filling the other half flattens
the profile and rebates the same amount. The cross-range cycle closes two ranges

subject: predict: gate the skew window and stop the escrow drifting below the potential (DBU-732)
body:
Two defects, both reachable once the rate is nonzero.

A mint recorded before the reference tick folded into an empty window, so the
accumulators stayed at zero while the book carried the order. Once anyone set the
reference tick the window became real, and closing that order subtracted a
nonzero amount from a zero accumulator and aborted — the position could not be
live-closed at all until settlement. The mint is gated instead, and only while
skew is on, so the shipped zero-rate path is unchanged.

The charge floored each leg independently while the potential floored once, so
cumulative collections fell below the potential by up to a unit per trade and the
backing assert could abort a legitimate trade. Take the difference of floored
potentials instead: collections then telescope to the current potential exactly,
which is what the escrow invariant claims. A three-mint sequence at a rate small
enough to truncate pins it, and fails against the previous arithmetic.

Cover the escrow the way the inventory-impact escrow is covered: isolation from
free cash and required cash, a rebate drawing only on its own reserve, the
over-spend abort, and the settlement release. Cover both new config bounds,
including the window fraction's floor, which unlike the rates sits well above
zero because a window with no ticks disables the statistic silently.

Add getters for the escrow and the quote's skew amounts, without which a flow
test cannot read either, and extend the flow helpers' backing assertion to the
skew reserve so it matches the contract rather than a weaker rule.

Pin the tenor scaling at an hourly cadence: a linear scaling truncates that
window to zero where the square root gives two ticks either side.

rationale: The commit fixes two arithmetic/logic defects that could cause escrow balances to drift below the required potential, leading to under-collection of funds and aborts of legitimate trades, which is a security-relevant loss of funds and denial‑of‑service. The added guard and corrected rounding restore the escrow invariant.

subject: predict: correct the variance-form rationale and drop an unreachable guard (DBU-732)
body:
The comment claimed the two-division variance form can floor below zero and needs
a clamp. It cannot: if m is floor(S1/n) then S2 >= S1^2/n >= m^2*n, so
floor(S2/n) >= m^2 and both forms are non-negative over the integers. That hazard
is real in floating point, not here. The single-division form is still the right
choice, for accuracy: dividing first discards each mean's fractional part before
squaring, an error of order max(W) rather than of order one. On a flat book at
1e12 per tick the two-division form reports a full DUSDC of deviation where the
true value is half a base unit.

ESkewVarianceTooWide cannot fire. The payout tree maintains prefixes in u64, so
the variance is at most max(W)^2 <= (2^64 - 1)^2, below u128::MAX, and its root
fits u64 exactly at the boundary. Shipping an abort code no test can reach is
worse than stating why the narrowing is total, so the guard is gone and the bound
is a comment. The remaining code renumbers to close the gap.

rationale: The commit only removes an unreachable error guard and updates documentation/comments; it does not change any observable behavior or fix a defect that could be exploited.

subject: predict: bound the skew rate so wing trades stay mintable and closable (DBU-732)
body:
The statistic is uniform over ticks while every amount it is checked against —
premium, redeem proceeds, the fee — is proportional to the contract's
probability. A marginal adjustment is rate * c * quantity with c at most a half,
so it does not scale with probability. Once rate * c passes a low-probability
contract's premium, two things break: the wing positions the mechanism exists to
encourage stop being mintable, and positions already held there stop being
closable. Both guards abort with no clamp, and because the charge and the
proceeds are both linear in quantity, a partial close does not help — the holder
has no exit until settlement.

Bound the rate at 0.5% rather than 100%. That keeps rate * c at or below a
quarter percent, half the default min_fee, so the ordinary fee dominates any
rebate: wing trades stay admissible, closes stay affordable, and harvesting the
escrow costs more in fees than it returns. The bound is relational, so the
comment names what widens and narrows it.

Record that the measure is direction-blind: trimming a peak and filling a dip
both flatten the profile and both earn a rebate, though only the first reduces
what the pool can owe. The rate ceiling is what keeps that rebate below the
trade's own fee.

Give the skew backing assertion a named error code; it was the only one of the
three that surfaced as an opaque abort.

rationale: The commit adds a hard bound to max_inventory_skew_rate (previously unbounded) to prevent aborts that made wing trades unmintable/unclosable, a condition that could be triggered to lock user funds and cause denial of service. This corrects a defect and mitigates a security-relevant availability issue.

subject: predict: make the skew escrow senior to the fee, and cover the flow
body:
A close clamps its trading fee at the payout it is charged against, because an
expiry-ramped fee can exceed a deep out-of-the-money redeem and a close must
never cost more than it releases. The skew charge was stacked on top of that
clamp and asserted afterwards, so any skew charge on such a close aborted rather
than collected, stranding a position the clamp exists to keep closable.

The escrow backs future rebates rather than being protocol revenue, so it is the
senior claim: the charge now comes out of the payout first and the fee is clamped
against what remains. `ESkewChargeExceedsCloseProceeds` survives for the residual
case where the charge exceeds the whole payout, which needs a leg worth less than
the charge; that position settles at expiry for what it is worth. RP-29 records
the response and the ordering.

Adds end-to-end coverage for the mechanism, which previously had none: the mint
charge and its escrow, a mint that flattens the book being paid, a close that
unbalances it being charged, partial-close telescoping, settlement release, the
event fields, and both boundaries above. The mint-side mirror code is unreachable
at any admissible rate, and a bounds test pins the margin that keeps it so.

subject: predict: cover skew and capital occupancy running together
body:
Nothing exercised both mechanisms at once: the skew tests ran with the impact
rate at zero and the impact tests with the skew rate at zero, so their
interaction was argued rather than measured.

The new test enables both and pins what it found. The two legs of a complete set
are disjoint, so the peak `M` never moves while `T` doubles, and occupancy —
reading `L = M + lambda(T - M)` — charges the *balancing* mint more than the
concentrating one. Skew reverses that ordering, which is the reason the second
mechanism exists; the test asserts the inversion directly rather than describing
it. It also pins that the escrows do not alias and that both potentials
telescope to zero over the same round trip, where neither leg nets zero alone.

subject: predict: pin that skew outweighs the occupancy rebate at the calibrated rates
body:
Closing the balancing leg of a complete set leaves the book one-sided, so
occupancy pays a rebate for a trade that makes the pool riskier. Skew has to be
the larger of the two for the net to come out a charge.

Whether it is depends entirely on the rate ratio, and the exaggerated rates the
other tests use to make escrow movements legible reverse the answer: at 20%
occupancy against 0.5% skew the rebate is five times the charge, and the pool
pays to be unbalanced. At the calibrated 0.1% and 0.13% the charge is ten times
the rebate. Both are asserted as hand-derived amounts so a rate change that
flips the ordering fails here rather than in production.

subject: predict: correct the partial-close and blast-radius claims for the skew abort
body:
Two statements about `ESkewChargeExceedsCloseProceeds` were wrong.

`decisions.md` said a partial close does not help "because charge and proceeds
are both linear in quantity". The charge is convex in the closed quantity, not
linear, so smaller closes are never worse per unit and are strictly better
whenever the profile is uneven across the closed range. The conclusion survives
for the case that actually reaches the abort — a book already flat across the
window, where the charge is exactly linear — but the stated reason did not, so
it now names the condition. A test closes a tenth of the stranded leg and pins
that it aborts the same way.

RP-29 said no other user's flow is blocked. The charge is a function of global
book state, so a third party who shapes the window between a holder's quote and
execution can flip a close from rebated to charged and push it past the bound.
The blast radius now says so, along with what bounds it: the stranded value is
near zero by construction and settles in full at expiry, so the harm is denial
of an early exit rather than loss.

subject: predict: fold the skew accumulators once per trade, and report the window
body:
The accumulators were computed twice on every trade: once in `inventory_skew`
to price the adjustment, where the result was discarded, and again in
`commit_skew_terms` to store it. Each pass ran `range_payout_sum`, so every mint
and close paid for two extra O(log n) traversals of the payout tree.

`inventory_skew` now returns a `SkewTerms` carrying both the priced adjustment
and the accumulator state the trade implies, and the terms structs carry it
through to the mutation, which writes it back. At a zero rate the terms carry
the values already stored, so the write-back is unconditional rather than a
branch. This also removes an ordering requirement rather than restating it: the
fold had to run before the payout tree mutated, and now the read is already done
by the time the terms exist.

`ReferenceTickSet` gains the window bounds the tick determines. A window that
rounds to nothing is otherwise indistinguishable on chain from a balanced book —
both show an empty escrow and a stream of zero adjustments — and the fixture's
own defaults land in that regime, which two tests now pin from opposite sides.

The relational bound between the skew rate and the premium floor is left to
`max_skew_rebate_stays_below_the_minimum_premium` rather than a runtime assert.
Both sides are upgrade-required constants and the test checks the rate ceiling
against the premium *floor*, so it is strictly stronger than a guard reading the
configured value, and it costs no permanently-frozen error code. The reasoning
now sits on the constant.

rationale: The commit changes the computation of skew accumulators to run only once per trade and removes an ordering requirement, fixing a functional inefficiency/bug. No security-relevant checks or protections are added, and the diff shows only performance and correctness adjustments without addressing exploitable conditions.

subject: predict: pin that a missing reference tick bricks a market's mint surface
body:
`assert_skew_window_ready` gates every mint on the reference tick once the skew
rate is nonzero. The tick comes from the exact Pyth print at the market's open,
which can simply be absent, and the rate is snapshotted at creation with no
admin path reaching a live market's config. The result is a market that holds
its pool allocation, can never be minted on, and has no way back.

The gate is not the defect and must stay: without it a pre-window mint folds
nothing into the accumulators while the book carries the order, and the matching
close then subtracts from zero and underflows, stranding that position instead.
What is missing is a recovery path, which `move.md` requires for exactly this
shape of bound. The test records the failure so the fix has something to turn
green.

rationale: The commit only adds a new test function; no production code is changed. It records a failure scenario but does not modify behavior, so it is not a bug fix nor a security fix.

subject: predict: stop the escrow seniority from diverting fee revenue to the closer
body:
Making the skew charge senior clamped the fee at `redeem_amount - skew_charge`.
That is wrong whenever the close would have succeeded without the reorder: the
escrow is funded from the payout under either ordering, so the fee reduction does
not reach it — it reaches the trader. With occupancy enabled the precondition is
the normal case, because a close's impact rebate is ordinarily far larger than
the skew charge.

The cap is now `min(redeem_amount, gross_proceeds - skew_charge)`. The first term
is the pre-existing rule that the fee is charged against the payout and never
against the trader's own returning escrow; the second makes the charge senior. It
binds only when the payout alone cannot cover both, so the deep out-of-the-money
close the reorder exists for still lands, and a close whose rebate absorbs the
charge pays exactly the fee it would have paid without skew.

Every existing test ran at a zero impact rate, where the two clampings are
indistinguishable. The new test enables both mechanisms with the fee floor at its
ceiling so the clamp binds, and pins the trader's net; the previous clamping
fails it by the diverted amount.

Also corrects three recorded claims that did not match the code: that the
reordering was value-neutral, that a partial close never helps (it does once the
concave impact rebate is on), and that the close-side bound is against the payout
rather than against everything the close releases.

subject: predict: bound the skew rate against the fee floor, which admins can zero
body:
The rate ceiling's safety argument is that the ordinary fee dominates any rebate,
so harvesting the escrow stays unprofitable. That argument names `min_fee` — and
`min_min_fee` is zero, so an admin can set the floor under the rebate ceiling
without tripping any bound. At a zero floor the fee on a 1%-probability contract
is 0.199% against a 0.25% rebate ceiling, and flattening the book pays more than
it costs.

`snapshot` now refuses the pairing: a rebate is bounded by `rate * quantity / 2`
and the fee below by `min_fee * quantity`, since the `base_fee * sqrt(p(1-p))`
term vanishes at both probability extremes, so the rate may not exceed twice the
floor. Checked at runtime rather than pinned by a test because, unlike the
premium relation whose both sides are upgrade-required constants, this one is
reachable through admin config. Tested through the real admin setters at the
boundary and one unit past it.

Also records the escrow invariant, which was asserted in code and absent from
`invariants.md`, and completes the mint and redeem formulas in the public fee
doc, which still omitted both skew legs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit adds a runtime check preventing the skew rate from exceeding twice the fee floor, fixing a bug where admins could set a zero fee floor and earn profit from flattening the book, which could be exploited to drain escrow funds. This is a missing input validation leading to economic loss.

subject: predict: widen the default skew window to 15% on measured escape rates
body:
The 10% anchor was sized on a sigma-coverage argument. Replay over Feb-Jun 2026
BTC says coverage there is 3.8 sigma rather than the assumed 5, and that realised
escapes run 40-90x the Gaussian rate at that width because the return
distribution's excess kurtosis is 19-23 at minute cadences. Sizing this window
off sigma and a normal tail was the calibration error.

Escape matters more than it looks, because the window is frozen at creation: once
spot leaves it the statistic decays and under-charges for the rest of the
market's life, with no way to re-centre. Path escape falls from 1.67% to 0.44%
per market going 10% to 15%, and from 4.25% to 1.33% in the most volatile month;
the daily cadence goes to zero.

It is nearly free because widening the window barely moves the charge. A
one-sided digital runs to the end of the ladder, so the fraction of the window it
covers does not change when the window widens - measured, 10% to 20% moves the
mean charge by 1.03-1.10x for digital flow and 0.84x for bounded-range flow, not
the 1/sqrt(N) a fixed-width range would suggest. Window and rate are therefore
near-independent levers: size the window on escape, the rate on steering.

Measurements recorded under predeploy/evidence.

subject: predict: add the entropic inventory statistic
body:
Adds the arithmetic for an inventory charge built on the certainty-equivalent
cost of the pool's payout book under exponential utility, weighted by the
risk-neutral probability of each settlement price:

    D(W) = b * ln( sum q(S) * exp(W(S)/b) )  -  sum q(S) * W(S)

Nothing calls it. The module owns the statistic and its incremental fold; the
accumulators and the range reads they need are a separate change.

The shape is chosen for two properties the mean-plus-standard-deviation form
cannot have. Adding a payout at every settlement price raises the certainty
equivalent and the fair value by the same amount, so buying every outcome is
free — asserted exactly, not within a tolerance. And because a trade's total is a
convex combination of the fair value and the certainty equivalent, both monotone,
no rate in [0, 1] can price a strictly worse book lower; the deviation form
admits no such rate once the settlement ladder is fine, because its monotonicity
bound is set by the smallest bucket on it.

The statistic is a difference of two independently floored terms and Jensen puts
the true difference at or above zero, so a book that owes the same everywhere can
leave the logarithm a unit short. That case clamps rather than aborts, and the
clamp can only bind within the rounding error of a book carrying no unevenness.

`exp` cannot return a value outside `u64`, so the exponent is bounded well inside
its input ceiling. Deriving the risk tolerance from the market's allocation keeps
the ratio inside that bound by construction rather than by hoping, which is the
wiring the next change owes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit introduces a new module and tests, adding a new statistic without modifying existing behavior; it does not appear to correct a defect, so it is not a bug fix nor a security fix.

subject: predict: add the probability-weighted inventory statistic
body:
Adds the arithmetic for an inventory charge on the spread of the pool's payout
book, counting each settlement price by how likely it is rather than equally:

    D(W) = sqrt( sum q(S)*W(S)^2 - ( sum q(S)*W(S) )^2 )

Nothing calls it. The module owns the statistic and its fold; the accumulators
and the range reads they need are a separate change.

Weighting by probability is what removes the window. Counting every tick equally
over an unbounded ladder is meaningless, so the unweighted form has to bound it,
and then owns a parameter that has to be sized, frozen in the right place, kept
above one tick of resolution, and re-derived whenever it changes because the
charge scales with the window's width. A price the market will almost certainly
never reach contributes almost nothing here without being excluded, so none of
that exists.

Both totals are plain sums with no division, so the fold is exact: a range opened
and closed returns them bit for bit, and splitting a trade into pieces reaches
the same totals as making it whole. Both are asserted.

rationale: The commit introduces a new module and tests for weighted inventory statistics; it does not modify existing code or fix previously incorrect behavior, so it is a feature addition rather than a bug fix.

subject: predict: wire the probability-weighted inventory charge end to end (DBU-732)
body:
The statistic module now carries its totals raw — payout times 1e9-scaled
mass, division deferred to the read — so a fold is integer sums and products
with no division at all. The previous form divided inside the fold and
floored differently on open and close: fifty open-close cycles at a payout
and mass whose product does not divide left an empty book scoring 273,861.
Raw carriage makes the round trip exact by construction, and the ragged
regression pins it.

The payout index stores each boundary's frozen weight and carries
mass-weighted first moments per subtree, so range_weighted_payout_sum
resolves a range's sum(q*W) in O(log n) by the same two reads
range_max_payout performs — the weighted analog of a tick-weighted first
moment, with the frozen survival function replacing the tick coordinate,
which is also what makes unbounded legs finite.

The measure freezes from the first mint's own validated pricer, atomically
with that mint: the book is empty at the freeze by construction, no admin
step or keeper exists, and a market whose snapshotted rate is zero never
evaluates a weight. Charges and rebates are differences of the floored
potential rate * D(W), so collections telescope to the current potential
exactly; the escrow is isolated in skew_reserve, senior to fee revenue on
the close path (RP-29 owns that ordering), and released at settlement.

Flow tests drive the custody end to end: a complete set's second leg is
rebated the first leg's charge exactly, a round trip across an oracle move
refunds to the unit, a close that unbalances a flat book is charged through
the clamp chain and the drain refunds it, and settlement releases the
residual.

subject: predict: remove the capital-occupancy charge in favor of the skew charge (DBU-732)
body:
The inventory-impact mechanism is removed end to end: the occupancy potential
phi(L) and its liability reads, the snapshotted impact scale, the isolated
impact reserve and its credit/pay/release custody, the charge and rebate terms
and quote fields, the config rate with its bounds and template setter, the
event fields, and the payout tree's complement_max_payout read that existed
only for the potential. The probability-weighted skew charge is the one
inventory mechanism: the close path's gross proceeds are redeem plus the skew
rebate, and an expiry's cash floor is payout liability plus the skew reserve.

The two mechanisms priced different objects — occupancy priced gross cash
held, skew prices the payout profile's shape — and running both means two
escrows and a joint calibration for a combined cost that is harder to reason
about than either part. One inventory charge is the product decision; skew is
the one with the measured risk signal. Nothing prices capacity occupancy now:
the per-cadence max_expiry_allocation funding cap in pool accounting is the
surviving control, and the decision record names capacity squatting as the
reopen condition. RP-30 carries the duty inventory for every deleted guard;
survivor error codes close their gaps per the pre-deploy rule.

LiveOrderRedeemed loses inventory_impact_rebate, MarketCreated and the
template config-history event lose inventory_impact_max_rate, and the four

subject: predict: re-anchor the inventory measure to the live forward (DBU-732)
body:
The measure's shape stays frozen from the market's first priced mint, but its
centre is now re-read from every later trade's own forward. Freezing both went
stale as soon as spot moved: a few standard deviations out, every strike the
market can still trade sits in a tail the frozen measure calls near-impossible,
so the charge decayed toward zero exactly when the book was accumulating
one-sided risk — tracking of remaining-life risk falls from 0.94 to 0.40 once
spot has travelled three sigma, and recovers to 0.94 when only the centre
moves, against 0.96 for a fully live measure. Only the shape needs the
volatility surface; the centre is already in every trade's validated pricer, so
re-anchoring needs no keeper.

Re-anchoring is free because the measure is mirrored on a lattice uniform in
log price: moving the centre translates the mass profile along that axis, which
is an integer cell shift of the stored cumulative masses. No surface is read
after the lattice is built, and mass that shifts past an end folds into that
end's sentinel, so the measure still sums to one under any anchor. The book is
mirrored as rise/fall difference arrays, so a trade touches two entries however
many cells it spans, and one scan recovers the profile and both moment pairs.

The charge is charge-only. A rebate is coherent only when both legs see the
same measure, and re-anchoring moves it between trades, so a refund computed
under a later centre would not be the amount collected. That deletes the
escrow, its rebate guards, the close-path seniority ordering and the abort it
needed (RP-29, retired in place): the charge is ordinary expiry surplus, junior
to every ordinary deduction, and can never block a close. The payout tree
returns to being purely the payout and backing index.

Sized at 256 cells across +/-10 at-the-money volatilities, which the
discretisation study puts at about 1% median error against the exact continuous
statistic. Measured cost: ~39k instructions per steady-state mint against Seb's
grid at ~128k, plus a one-time ~254k lattice build on the market's first mint.
rationale: [MEV] The commit removes the inventory‑skew escrow and re‑anchors the inventory measure, fixing a defect where the charge decayed to zero when spot moved, allowing under‑charging of risk. This could be exploited by moving the spot price to avoid fees, leading to financial loss, thus a security‑relevant bug. The changes to code and docs (removing inventoryReserve fields and escrow logic) constitute a behavior fix with security impact.

subject: predict: capture the valuation snapshot in place instead of journaling it
body:
The staged flush recovered each market's snapshot-instant NAV by recording
every mid-window trade into a per-market delta log and replaying it backwards
over the live rows at valuation. That shape carried three costs: an equivalence
obligation (the adjusted walk had to reproduce the snapshot walk's rounding,
clamping, and monotonicity observation bit-for-bit), a per-market trade budget
(a full log froze that market's trading until valued, max_valuation_log_ops),
and a recording hook on every mutation source that had to be enumerated rather
than covered structurally.

The snapshot is now captured where it lives (the shape prototyped in #1268).
The stamp copies the two cash rows NAV reads eagerly at the snapshot instant.
The payout tree holds its own snapshot keyed by the flush ordinal: each node
copies its boundary quantities into a shadow immediately before its first
mutation under that generation — an untouched node is its own snapshot, a node
created after the snapshot carries zero shadows, and a node emptied mid-window
is retained as a live-zero husk. snapshot_nav is then the same linear walk as
the live read over the captured terms, so the frozen mark's rounding and
monotonicity contract are identical by construction, and trades record nothing:
mid-window trading is unbudgeted.

Retention never outlives one window: every husk is removed by the same
value_expiry that consumes the snapshot (including husks stranded by an aborted
generation), husks convert existing nodes rather than adding any (the RP-30 cap
and its object budget are undisturbed), and the live walk skips them (a husk is
no live order's edge; the frozen walk that owns the tick still observes it). A
stale stamp discard also deactivates the tree snapshot, and a superseded
generation can never serve a frozen read.

Deleted: RangeDelta, fold_range_deltas, walk_linear_adjusted and its merge-join
(~330 lines), the begin/record trade hooks, record_maintenance_cash_delta, the
max_valuation_log_ops knob and its EValuationLogFull abort. The registers and
docs move with the code: RP-29(e) supersedes the log cap with the no-budget
shape, RP-30 restates the cap's meaning under husks, C-5 closes by construction
(no log compute term), and decisions.md records the mechanism and its rejected
alternatives.

subject: predict: store payout boundaries in an inline sorted vector
body:
Adopts the store prototyped in #1269 under the staged flush. Records live in
a tick-sorted vector on the market object — binary search and memmove replace
the AVL's rotations and subtree summaries, and the per-record snapshot shadows
ride on the records. The same five evaluators return the same exact terms.

A value_expiry now loads no per-strike children at all: the staged shape had
already removed C-1's joint budget by valuing one market per transaction, and
this removes the object-cache driver at the store, so the transaction's
binding budget is its own pricing compute. max_payout_tree_nodes is no longer
derived from the object budget (there are no children to budget); it stays at
960 as a compute-headroom literal until P-30's localnet remeasure prices the
inline walk, and C-2's children reserve closes as moot. The snapshot mechanism
simplifies with the structure: capture sits at the single non-recursive
mutation site, and release_snapshot's husk purge is one compaction pass.

Registers and docs move with the code: RP-30 restates the cap's basis, C-2 is
resolved by restructure, and the decisions register records the store change
with its rejected alternatives (the single-PTB flush over this store, which

subject: predict: remove the permissionless settled redeem (DBU-760)
body:
`expiry_market::redeem_settled_permissionless` let any sender close another
account's settled position using Predict-derived app auth. It is deleted, along
with its only helper `predict_account::generate_auth_as_app`. `redeem_settled`
with account `Auth` is now the sole settled exit.

The entrypoint predates leverage, staking, and the trading-loss rebate and
outlived all three. Nothing calls it: no off-chain component builds the call,
and the only in-repo callers were the test fixture and the gas harness. What it
still did was hand the position's storage deposit to whoever sent the
transaction, since Sui credits the storage rebate to the sender. The payout
credits the position's own account either way, and the holder is paid the same
rebate for redeeming themselves.

Removing it also drops Predict's standing package-level authority to mutably
load any account: `generate_auth_as_app` was its only call into the account
registry's app-auth gate, so `authorize_app`/`deauthorize_app` no longer affect
any Predict flow. `PredictApp` survives only as the witness namespacing
Predict's data slot, which `attach`/`borrow_data_mut` accept on a permit alone.

Nothing on-chain reclaims a settled position now. No flow depends on that: a
settled redeem moves `balance` and `required_cash` by the same integer, so pool
free cash is invariant under it, and the settled sweep deactivates the expiry
and materializes profit whether or not any position is redeemed. The positions
table is only ever read by key.

The settled-redeem test helper and the cleanout gas harness are retargeted to
account auth rather than deleted, so the storage-rebate-vs-compute measurement
still runs against the incentive that now governs reclamation — the holder's.
The two tests whose subject was the app-auth gate are removed; their payout and
cash assertions are already covered by
`explicitly_settled_redeem_pays_terminal_payout`. The simulation parity oracle
no longer encodes a per-redemption auth mode.

Duty inventory for the deleted entrypoint: `predeploy/response-policies.md`
RP-29. RP-11's retirement note claimed the cleanout survived this removal and is
corrected.
rationale: only non-code files changed

subject: predict: correct the settled-redeem trust model and pin the sweep claim
body:
Two doc claims added by the previous commit were wrong about the account
package. `account_registry::authorize_app` takes `&AccountAdminCap` and its own
doc says it "globally authorizes"; `load_account_mut` under `AUTH_APP` "carries
no owner or operation restriction". So an authorized app is authorized by the
protocol admin for every account at once, not by an owner for their own, and it
needs no owner consent to act. The `redeem_settled` doc and the concepts page
said otherwise; both are corrected.

The same error reached RP-29, which credited the deleted entrypoint with having
given holders "a real per-account opt-out" through `deauthorize_app`. There was
never such an opt-out — the switch is global and admin-gated, so a holder could
not decline. That strengthens the removal rather than weakening it, and the
entry now says so.

RP-29's second duty bullet is the claim that makes the removal safe for the
pool: an unredeemed settled position strands no pool-claimable cash. It was
pinned by `explicit_settlement_then_standalone_rebalance_sweeps_market`, which
never mints, so it proved the sweep works with no position rather than with an
outstanding one. Adds `settled_sweep_retains_payout_backing_for_an_unredeemed_winner`:
mint a winner, settle, sweep without redeeming, assert the market keeps back
exactly the payout and the expiry deactivates, then redeem and assert the holder
is still paid in full. Both tests are now pinned.

Also: RP-11 still named the two deleted tests as currently pinning the app-auth
gate; the access-control audit lens still listed settled redeem as a
permissionless path; the localnet bootstrap still authorized `PredictApp` on the
registry, which has been a no-op for Predict since the data slot only ever
needed a bare permit. The zero-payout guard's comment justified itself with the
permissionlessness this branch removed, and the standing app-auth decision
record was rewritten in place rather than annotated with a dated pointer.

subject: predict: freeze the vault-side figures at the seal
body:
The mark was assembled from two instants: per-market cash frozen at each
stamp, vault figures (idle, the profit basis, the pending protocol cut)
read live at the finish. Bridging them took a maintenance-ordering
record reversed out of three terms, and forced the standalone settled
sweep to defer for the whole window.

settled members are swept inside the snapshot stage so their cash is in
idle by the capture, the seal freezes the four vault figures, and
finish_flush prices purely from frozen state. The maintenance recorder,
its reversal arithmetic, and the sweep deferral all delete — an
in-window cash move can no longer reach the mark, so there is nothing
to correct for. value_expiry now moves no cash for any member.

The one new refusal: rebalance_expiry_cash aborts while the snapshot
stage is still open (ESnapshotStageOpen) — a cross-move between a stamp
and the seal's capture would put the moved cash in both figures or
neither. The stage is a single transaction, so only the flush-starter's
own PTB can compose that state; the keeper's snapshot PTB does not.
